The author's stated purpose is not to analyze the specific advantages or disadvantages of the "Free State" created by the treaty, nor to critique its founders. The author notes that these founders were once considered champions of the Republic but now seem dedicated to its suppression.

Instead, a single principle for judgment is offered: if the British government strongly supports the "Free State," which it appears to do, then people who are sincere, selfless supporters of Ireland, truth, and justice should oppose it.

The justification for this view is that Britain's long history of breaking treaties and engaging in hypocrisy demonstrates that the British government and its people cannot have genuinely honest or unselfish interests in Ireland's welfare.
styled: Now it is not the object of this correspondent to discuss the merits or the demerits of the treaty-proffered "Free State", or that of its pro- moters and founders -- one time acknowledged Champions of the Republic which now they seem to have given their lives to suppress. I will only say this just now, in favor of the same or against them; if Britain is in favor of the said "Free State" - and she seems to mightily so-then, honest, un- selfish, lovers of Ireland, and of truth, and of justice, ought to be opposed to it. Why? Because as centuries of Britain-broken Treaties, and British hypocrisy make manifest - the English government or the people composing it cannot be honestly or unselfishly interested in Ireland.

To understand a political conflict in Ireland, even without knowing the specific details of the factions involved, one can analyze the situation by asking a single question: Which side does the British government support? The underlying premise is that, based on the history of British involvement, the side favored by Britain is the one that serves British interests rather than the one representing genuine Irish independence.

This principle is applied to the contemporary conflict between the established Irish Republic and the newer Irish Free State. The passage claims that the creators of the Free State intended for it to subtly replace the Republic with a system modeled on and favorable to British interests.

The author concludes that the answer to which side Britain supports is so obvious that it would be considered naive or extremely uninformed to even have to ask. It is suggested that any observer, regardless of their own affiliation or level of education, would immediately know which faction has British backing.
styled: Consequently if your correspondent knew absolutely nothing of the claims or the aims of any faction in Ireland - or of any party in Ireland -- for example just now, the legitimately established Republic and the said free-state, which later as its authors evidently hoped, was to sneak real British - fashioned into the place of the former, he would simply point to the history of British interest in Ireland and ask the one little question: "On which side of the dispute is British Favor?" The writer's father visited on the 10th of the month and reported that everyone at home is well. The father also conveyed that the letter's recipient, Ella, seems lonely, in part because her location is far from a church.

The writer advises Ella to be patient with her current circumstances, to pray, and to maintain hope. This advice is based on the example of their mother, who endured significant hardships with patience and acceptance while living at places called the River-bank and Trimbelle. After many years, their father now reflects on those past difficulties with a sense of deep spiritual comfort. The writer presents the contrast between their parents' past struggles and their current positive situation as evidence of beneficial divine guidance, expressing a hope that their parents' lives will continue to improve.

Based on this perspective, the writer argues that Ella's current hardships are preferable to a life of material wealth, even if that wealth allowed her to live in close proximity to a church and the sacraments. The central claim is that enduring these trials provides greater long-term safety and security for Ella and her family. This positive outcome, however, is conditional on her continuing to perform religious duties, such as acts of contrition and other related practices.
styled: Father was here on the 10th and all are well at home, thanks be to God! He said that you seemed to be lonesome out there, being so far from church etc. Well Dear Ella, I only pray you to content yourself for the present and pray and hope-even as you know poor dear Mother did, at the River-bank & at Trimbelle. You must know that there were trials in those places and indeed patience & resignation exercised. Now after so many years Father speaks of great consolation. It is really enough to draw a tear of admiration and gratitude for God's merciful providence, if one only considers the past (of our dear Parents) and now beholds their present circumstances and prospects. May their sky continue to brighten as their end approaches. For my part dear Sister I congratulate you on your present trials much rather than if you were "prospering" in riches even within a block of the Most Blessed Sacrament. I think you and yours are safer, especi- ally in the long run. If you only make your acts of contrition, etc.

The writer expresses thanks for an Easter card, which was meaningful because it contained the first picture of the writer's patron saint they had ever received. In return, the writer sends good wishes to the recipient and all the people at a location called Graymoor.

The main purpose of the communication is to commend the recipient for a protest they made to the plaintiff's attorneys regarding a church property case at Graymoor. The writer sees the values expressed in this protest as being authentically Franciscan and Christian.

The writer is confident that many justice-loving people, including Christians of other denominations who read about the protest in a publication called "the Lamp," will speak out to prevent the community from being evicted from Graymoor, viewing such an act as a major injustice.

Finally, the writer states an opinion that any reasonable person with Christian values who understands the facts and circumstances of the Graymoor case would inevitably agree with the recipient's position and recognize it as the correct Christian stance.
styled: Please accept my sincere thanks for the little card you sent with Easter greetings. It is the first picture of my dear Patron I have ever received. Be sure also that I here- with return similar good wishes for yourself and for all at Graymoor. I take this occasion also Dear Sister, to assure you that I thanked Almighty God - and do thank Him for hav- ing inspired some one with such truly Franciscan sentiments as were manifest in your gentle protest to the plaintiff at- tornies of that Graymoor Church property case. I am fully con- fident that there are too many upright lovers of justice even among our separated brothers and sisters who read the Lamp and paused at that letter ever to hold their peace while an act of such injustice were perpetrated as would be perpetrated should your community be ejected from Graymoor. In my opinion there is no sane man who has a spark of Christianity who will hesi- tate when he knows the facts and the present circumstances at and around Graymoor, to second these sentiments - and acknow- ledge your sentiments as really Christian.

The Father Superior, who has been ill with a severe cold for approximately two weeks, wishes to express sympathy to the Sisters for their recent eviction.

The eviction is characterized as unreasonable and unjust, made possible by unscrupulous individuals exploiting a rigid application of the law. The author is confident that the majority of people from other Christian denominations will condemn this action, which was supposedly done in their name, and will regret it. The author's community had hoped that such an event, which they view as a violation of justice and charity, would not occur.

From a theological perspective, the passage suggests that such worldly victories are temporary because human plans are ultimately subject to a divine will. It asserts that God has allowed these events to happen as part of a larger design to bring a positive outcome from a negative situation.

The Sisters are advised to find comfort and encouragement in the religious teaching that those who are unjustly insulted and persecuted for their faith are considered blessed. Based on the same religious authority, the passage concludes that the best course of action for the Sisters is to pray sincerely for those who have persecuted them.
styled: Rev. Father Superior who has been in with a severe cold for about two weeks wished me to convey our sympathy to the Sisters on account of the unreasonable and unjust eviction which the "killing letter of the law" has enabled unscrupulou men to score against them. - an eviction which we are confi- dent the great majority of our separated brethern will con- demn as done in their name and will regret. Needless to say we all hoped that things would never come to such a farce a- gainst common justice and charity. However, the victories of the world are short-lived- "man proposes but God disposes." We may be sure that Almighty God has not permitted things to take such a course without some good design of His own - to turn evil into good. At all events the words of our Divine Master, "Blessed are ye when they shall revile you and per- secute you ... unjustly for my sake .... ", should be a consola- tion to you and an encouragement. The sisters will hardly be able to do anything better than to pray earnestly for their persecutors, according to the same divine authority.

The writer provides the following information and advice:

The recipient should not be worried about the frequency of their oral confessions or their practice of Spiritual Communion. The recipient is also asked to ensure that the "Mass-prayers" from a place called Trimbelle are imitated. A person named Owney should also be encouraged to adopt this practice, as should their neighbors, even those who are not Catholic.

The writer makes a personal request to be remembered sometimes when the recipient prays the rosary.

Regarding personal news, the writer reports having been made a sub-deacon on December 8th and anticipates being ordained as both a deacon and a priest before August. The writer expresses a hope that their superiors' decisions will be divinely guided and that God's will is done.

The writer explains that permission and materials for this letter were provided by a superior, who also sent along a small picture for the recipient.

Greetings are conveyed to Brother Thomas (Traynor), Owen, and everyone else, along with a message of affection for the children.

Finally, the recipient is instructed to urge Brother Owney not to neglect the beneficial practice of giving aid to the poor and to orphans.

The passage makes the following points:

1.  **Context and Standards:** The author begins by establishing a set of standards for Catholic media. These are based on a recent appeal by Pope Pius X for an effective Catholic press and the sincere efforts of capable publishers. This ideal is contrasted with the secular press, which is broadly accused of mixing fact with fiction, appealing to base emotions, and being fundamentally hostile to justice and truth.

2.  **Primary Criticism:** Given this context, the author expresses regret that some publications identified as "Catholic" show a dependence on sources with atheistic viewpoints.

The author notes that the recipient gave significant space to Lord Shaw's quote, which advised people not to be disturbed by rumors because "Ireland is on the way to Peace." The author interprets this as deceptive language, or propaganda, designed to placate a concerned American audience. It is suggested that this statement is part of a coordinated and polished media campaign by British agencies and newspapers.

The central argument is that the meaning of the word "peace" is not clear and must be questioned. The author challenges whether Lord Shaw's perspective is inspired by the President of Ireland (representing the Irish Republican cause) or the Prime Minister of England (representing British interests).

The author then defines two opposing types of peace:
1.  A "Cromwellian Peace," which refers to peace achieved through violent conquest and the subjugation of the Irish people.
2.  The peace sought by Irish Republicans, which is genuine independence and for which martyrs like Patrick Pearse, Terence MacSwiney, Cathal Brugha, and Harry Boland died.

The author's clear implication is that Lord Shaw is predicting the first kind of peace—one imposed by British force—rather than the true peace of Irish sovereignty.

The widespread mourning in Britain for Michael Collins is a revealing indicator of whether his death should be considered "A SAD BLOW FOR IRELAND."

The author distinguishes between two "falls" experienced by Collins. The first was a political fall in December when he signed the Anglo-Irish Treaty (the "London Pact"). This action is described as causing him to lose his status as an Irish patriot and become a "Hero Irishman" in the eyes of the English.

The second fall was his actual death eight months later, which occurred while he was working to advance the interests of that same treaty. The author notes that some would argue he was also advancing British interests. This death placed him permanently beyond any potential British influence.

The author's central argument is that the intensity of the British grief over his death provides a satisfactory way to measure how much of a loss it truly was for Ireland. The implication is that if the British considered his death a major blow to their interests, it may not have been a blow to Ireland's.

This analysis of Collins's death is used to illustrate a broader point: there is more information available about the true nature of the Anglo-Irish relationship than what is being reported by most newspaper editors. The author suggests that these editors, while otherwise honest, seem unconcerned with this deeper perspective. The prevailing view of the Irish situation is characterized as a narrative shaped by powerful media interests, specifically referred to as "the Northlif-Hearst and Co."

This specific concern is part of a broader critique of modern civilization, which is described as suffering from a profound lack of understanding. The author draws a parallel: while contemporary people may find the biblical first humans to be naive for being deceived by the serpent, modern society is itself blind. This power is identified as the force behind the modern press. The press is labeled "blasphemous" on the grounds that it is fundamentally hostile to justice and truth. The argument continues that since God is the eternal embodiment of both justice and truth, the press is therefore hostile to God. A 1902 encyclical by Pope Leo XIII is referenced to support this assertion.

The passage concludes that modern society, whether considering itself civilized or not, generally acts as if this malevolent spiritual force is nothing more than a childish myth. The author finds this dismissal to be incomprehensible.

It is observed that people often express surprise at the perceived naivety and susceptibility of the first humans to temptation. However, despite scientific and historical advancements, the author asserts that people fail to recognize, or even suspect, the presence of a malevolent power, akin to the biblical serpent, operating through contemporary media, which the author describes as blasphemous. The author strongly maintains that prominent contemporary media is blasphemous because it is fundamentally opposed to justice and truth, and consequently, to God, who is considered the eternal embodiment of both. This perspective is supported by a reference to an encyclical by Leo XIII (1902). The author concludes that people, regardless of their level of civilization, generally act as if this malevolent power is merely a fictional concept.

Yet, with all our science and with all the manifestation of historic ages, we refuse to recognize -- nay even to suspect-behind the blasphemous press of to-day, the same power that animated the wretched serpent. Aye, positively nothing less than blasphemous in the "Great Press" of to-day, because "Bitterly hostile to justice and truth" and therefore hostile to God himself who is eternally both. (See encyc'1 Leo XIII-1902) A civilized humanity, or as uncivilized, we act in general these days as though that power were nothing more than a childish myth. How?

The central claim is that millions of young men were sacrificed in a war for the principle of "Self-Determination." This principle is equated directly with the Catholic theological doctrine of "Free Will," which is described as a "God-given faculty."

A profound hypocrisy is identified: while claiming to uphold this principle, the nations of the world remain silent about the 74-day protest and subsequent death of Terence MacSwiney, which is termed a "martyrdom." They are also silent about the long-term suffering of his nation, described as an "age-long crucifixion." Both MacSwiney and his nation were protesting in the name of justice and the sacrifices made for self-determination. Their protest was against what is called an "astounding outrage"—an international attempt to destroy that very principle.

This silence is presented as evidence that "so-called civilization" is a sham and a farce. It is also said to prove that the Allied nations' stated reasons for their war against and treatment of Central Europe were "manifest hypocrisy." The situation is condemned as a clear outrage against intelligence and decency.

A warning is issued that nations and individuals should not be deceived, asserting that "God will not be mocked forever." The Allied nations and their civilization are accused of mocking both the honest people of the world and God.

Finally, the passage questions who is to blame for this situation and laments the absence of a strong, proactive Catholic press to champion the cause, concluding with a plea for divine help.

The author expresses a desire to prevent *The Catholic News*, and the honest press in general, from suffering a serious loss of credibility. This outcome is considered worse than any form of honest criticism and is seen as inevitable unless the press stops its tendency to favor British perspectives.

This pro-British bias is described in three forms:
1.  Promoting British viewpoints.
2.  Repeating British falsehoods or slanders ("calumnies").
3.  Spreading "British Colored Truths"—misleading or selectively presented information—which are considered the most dangerous.

The author argues that this issue is particularly relevant in light of the ongoing war in Ireland, which is characterized as having been started, supported, and waged by the British. In this context, a comparison is made between modern "colored truths" and the biblical story of the Serpent and Eve in Genesis 3:4.

The passage quotes the Serpent telling Eve, "No, you shall not die the death, for God doth know that in what day soever you shall eat thereof, your eyes shall be opened and you shall be as Gods, knowing good and evil."

This biblical statement is presented as a prime example of a "colored truth" and an unreliable prediction. While it was technically true that their eyes were opened, the resulting "vision" or knowledge was a negative and disastrous one, not the positive, god-like status that was implied. The author suggests that being deceived by modern "colored truths" leads to a similarly harmful outcome for everyone.
styled: He wishes simply to save, not only The Catholic News, but as much as he can, the honest press in general from humiliation more serious than any honest criticism could be, and that must come unless something be dore to arrest the above lamented in- clination of positively favoring British views, and British Calumnies, and worst of all because more dangerous, British Colored Truths. Who will doubt, at second thought and in the light of the present British-Begotten and British-fostered - and I must say British-waged War in Ireland that the above words of Lord Shaw are at least a weak parallel to those we find in the Third Chapter of Holy Writ? Here they follow: "And the Serpent said to the Woman: No, you shall not die the death, for God doth know that in what day soever you shall eat thereof, your eyes shall be opened and you shall be as Gods, knowing good and evil." (Gen. 111, 4) That is just an example of colored truth and of dubious prediction. No one doubts that their eyes were opened. But alas for their vision! and alas for your vision and mine!

The author suggests that history is repeating itself. A historical parallel is drawn to the case of Joan of Arc, who was condemned for witchcraft by a Catholic Bishop. This Bishop, reportedly acting under duress from the British, subjected her to extreme cruelty before she was burned at the stake as a heretic.

The author claims that, according to reports, one or two high-ranking church leaders in America are prepared to act similarly toward Irish patriots, even without being pressured by the British. Such actions are presented as a potential scandal.

The author then directly challenges the Bishop of Buffalo and the Archbishop of Baltimore, who have apparently claimed that "Eamon DeValera seems to have completely lost his reason." The author poses a rhetorical question: if De Valera's mental state has been affected, who is responsible? The answer provided is that the blame lies with the "despicable power"—implying the British—which the two church leaders now seem to support. This is the same power that De Valera has successfully resisted for four long and bitter years, a period of great suffering for both him and Ireland.

Finally, the author asserts that blame for the situation also lies with three other factors in addition to the aforementioned power: British hypocrisy, the silence of the international community, and the very leaders and guides previously mentioned.
styled: But history, it seems here as well as elsewhere, must repeat itself, It was a Bishop that condemned St. Joan of Arc for witchery and that a little later, durressed as he was by the British (and at that, time supposed to be a Catholic), exposed her to unmentionable cruelties and finally burned her at the stake as a heretic. If reports be true there are one or two pre- lates in America who would do the like for a number of Irish Joans, even without British duress. May the Good God deliver us from scandals! But I would ask his Lord- ship from Buffalo and his Grace from Baltimore if "Eamon DeValera seems to have completely lost his reason", who is to blame, if not the despicable power his own Grace and his lordship seem to be now espousing and that DeValera has frustrated, escaped and withstood these four years -- so long and so bitter for poor Ireland, and for DeValera? What is to blame after British hypocrisy more than the above mentioned international silence? More than the already referred to leaders and guides?

It is asserted as an undeniable fact that individual leaders have been and are guilty of criminal silence and mockery. These leaders are now seen to be escalating their wrongdoing. Instead of feeling personal and national shame that no moral authority has emerged to condemn hypocrisy—in the way the biblical figure Daniel did—some leaders are now openly aligning themselves with an aggressive and destructive national power.

These leaders are accused of engaging in detached, calculating debates over minor points of morality. This behavior, whether intentional or not, serves to divert attention from what is identified as the true source of the troubles in Ireland. This source is explicitly named as the presence of British soldiers and British corruption, a view attributed to a Dr. Ryan, E.G., in the publication "America."

This dynamic of focusing on trivialities while ignoring a much larger problem is compared to the biblical aphorism of "straining at a gnat, and swallowing a camel." Consequently, the leaders are condemned as "blind guides." The author acknowledges the harshness of the tone but distinguishes it from unproductive bitterness, stating that bitterness, like falsehood and exaggeration, is unhelpful to a just cause.
styled: Aye, God help us, and forgive us! They seem now, however, to be going further into crime. In- stead of blushing for shame, personal as well as national, that no one has a- risen like Daniel of old to convict the hypocrites, some of them are be- ginning to come out on the side of shame itself, on the side of the bull-dog and the lion -- the side of the arch-ravager of nations. The passage presents the following arguments and claims in support of Eamon DeValera:

1.  **DeValera's Condition and Support:** It is believed that DeValera remains mentally competent, a fact the author considers a near-miraculous act of divine intervention. He is said to have the backing of 30,000 patriotic soldiers who, despite being mostly unarmed, represent hope for achieving "Self Determination" and democracy in Ireland.

2.  **Theological Justification for Support:** The author constructs an argument based on religious principles. The core premise is that God supports the principle of self-determination. From this, the author concludes that the majority of people in Ireland must support the "soul of the Republic."

3.  **Majority Support for DeValera:** This argument is extended to assert that if God supports principle and the Irish Republic, then the majority of the Irish people must support DeValera. The author insists this is true, regardless of any reports, criticisms, or opposing forces that claim otherwise.

4.  **Prediction of Victory:** The author predicts that DeValera will ultimately triumph over all his enemies. This victory is attributed to his religious devotion, specifically his appeal to the Sacred Heart, which is compared to his situation when facing a death sentence in 1916. This triumph could even be achieved through martyrdom, in a way that is compared to the victory of a martyred saint.

A document, presented as a statement by Bishop Michael J. Gallagher regarding Eamon DeValera's visit to the United States, has been circulated, and a copy was sent to the publication "The Irish World."

The author of the passage congratulates "The Irish World" for its "dignified silence" or "prudent oversight" in not publishing or commenting on this document, viewing this inaction as appropriate for an experienced and responsible publication.

The author finds it difficult to believe that the statement is a carefully considered expression from Bishop Gallagher, a person they admire and believe to be a supporter of Ireland and justice. A possible explanation offered is that the Bishop may have been misled.

However, the author also considers that they might be deceiving themselves in thinking the best of the Bishop. They draw a parallel to an event ten months prior concerning a public split between an individual named Cohalan and DeValera. At that time, the author had expressed hope that Cohalan’s motives were not unworthy, but now implies that this hope was misplaced. This past experience of being wrong makes the author question their own judgment about Bishop Gallagher's motives.

The author concludes with the hope that, with time and honest public criticism, Bishop Gallagher might be prompted to express different views or clarify his position.

The author presents a defense of an Irish representative, identified as De Valera, for his refusal to compromise with the leaders of an American association.

The argument is structured as follows:

1.  **The Association's Hypocrisy:** The American association is officially defined as a group of citizens founded to help the Irish people achieve freedom. However, the author argues that the Irish representative is justified in refusing to even discuss a compromise with its leaders. The author claims that the group's members are not true "Friends of Ireland" but are more comparable to the historical "A.P.A." (American Protective Association), an anti-Catholic organization. This implies the group is acting against Irish interests despite its stated purpose.

2.  **The Unreasonable Fear of an Alliance:** The author characterizes the American group's fear of a potential Irish alliance with England as completely unreasonable and insincere. To illustrate its absurdity, this fear is compared to the A.P.A.'s historical fear of an alliance between the Pope and the forces of Hell.

3.  **Defense of De Valera:** The author defends De Valera against a specific criticism known as the "Cuban blunder." This accusation is dismissed as obvious slander. The author asserts that all of De Valera's subsequent statements and actions, including his difficult return to Ireland, serve as proof that the accusation was false.

4.  **The Meaninglessness of "Splitters":** The author concludes that accusations of causing division ("splitters") are irrelevant and meaningless. As long as the parties involved share the same fundamental objective, such accusations are considered empty talk.

A core principle is stated: when any individual, system, organization, or faction becomes more important than the cause it is meant to serve, one should disassociate from it. At that point, it is no longer beneficial and has begun to cause harm, regardless of its past accomplishments.

This idea, written in Rome on January 1, 1920, is presented as being relevant to a concern held by many members of an organization identified as the F.O.I.F. This concern is reportedly demonstrated by the large number of associated members in a related group, the A.A.R.I.R.

The author expresses a wish for the sincere members of both organizations, as well as the readers of *The Irish World and Industrial Liberator*, to be guided by unselfish justice, consistency, and genuine charity.

Finally, the author notes that space limitations prevent the printing of certain personal correspondence. The author is convinced that this correspondence would reveal the true source of a potential or developing conflict.

The writer explains that an enclosed, returned letter is a partial reason for their silence concerning the recipient's bereavement the previous August. The writer wants to assure the recipient that this silence did not mean they were not thinking about the loss.

The writer then presents a religious framework for understanding the death of the child, Owen. This perspective holds that one should trust that God has a merciful plan that will one day be revealed. According to this view, God permits suffering in all cases, including the recipient's, for the purpose of allowing children to come to heaven.

Based on this belief, the writer advises the recipient that they have a reason to be happy during the Christmas season. The specific reason given is the idea that their child, Owen, who was an altar boy, is now among the "holy Innocents" in heaven.

In closing, the writer simultaneously expresses condolences for the recipient's grief while also wishing them a holy and happy Christmas, based on the comforting theological perspective that has been offered.
styled: The returned letter herewith inclosed will partly explain my silence at your sorrows last August. But though silent, I have not been al- together unmindful of your bereavement. However we may confidently trust in God to manifest some day a merciful design - not only in your case of such sorrow but in every case where He has per- mitted suffering in order that little children may come to Him. How happy you ought to be in reality this holy season! to have your little Owen, not only an altar boy, but one of the great heavenly army of holy Innocents. In this thought, while in another sense I condole with you, I wish you a holy and a happy Blessed Christmastide!

With reflection, however, their appreciation for the connections has grown. styled: God bless you these unsettled days; you and yours. Many thanks for your kind favor of March 12th as also that of a few weeks back, as well as the letter you sent me before Christmas. A final note from Brooklyn, New York, on September 14, 1945, reports that Mrs. Nagle was present and in "perfect health."

The passage advises turning to God, asserting that God's concern for an individual's material and spiritual welfare is greater than any other source of care.

It recommends a method for building trust in God's divine providence:
1.  Approach God, specifically through Jesus, with simple, child-like humility, acknowledging one's status as one of God's children.
2.  Frequently thank God not only for past and present blessings but also in advance for any future suffering that God may permit. This gratitude should be for specific potential hardships, not just in general terms.
3.  Surrender everything entirely to God's will. This includes all life circumstances and the specific details of one's death—when, where, and how it will happen.

The passage claims that adopting this practice will bring a significant increase in peace and contentment. It concludes by stating that humble confidence in God is what spiritual adversaries fear most.

The central figure, the infant Jesus, is said to return at Christmas to free people from sorrow. His qualities of love, grace, and gentleness are an invitation for every individual to prepare a place for him in their hearts. His birth, power, and miracles are presented as proof that he is the Son of the Virgin, fulfilling an ancient prophecy. A hope is expressed that he will separate people from sin and its associated shame, and that he will have a permanent, central place in their hearts.

The purpose of human existence is defined as knowing God, a goal described as a blessing that is fulfilled by loving and serving him. For grateful people who value this relationship correctly, the experience is described as a taste of heaven on Earth, with a value equivalent to heaven itself.

A separate, personal message is intended for a child named Casey M. It states that he is now old enough to consider his eternal salvation, a task that should be viewed as both a responsibility and a privilege.

When conventional human and scientific help has failed, it is advised to pray to God. The passage claims that God is receptive to being asked for help. The recommended approach is to pray with confidence and to propose or vow to do something that is pleasing to God in exchange for a favorable outcome or a granted request.

The act of raising children to be good members of society is presented as an action that is highly pleasing to God. This applies equally to both biological and adopted children, as the passage suggests God is indifferent to how a family is formed. It is claimed that dedicated and faithful parents are given a special quality of love as a result.

To illustrate this, a biblical verse from Romans 11 is cited, which emphasizes that God's wisdom, knowledge, judgments, and methods are profound and beyond human comprehension.

Finally, the text states that a self-explanatory letter is being included. This enclosure is a copy of a letter from a Monsignor, which was provided by a Father Edward.

But, to even try to raise children for God and society is so manifestly pleasing to God - and this, whether they be procured by natural generation or by adoption ( seemingly quite a matter of indifference to Him), that He has given a specially beautiful color- ing to the love of those whose privilege it is to have become earn- est faithful parents. So that quite appropriately the song of the Psalmist may be here also applied: " ... O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and of the knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are His judgements and how unsearchable His ways!" (Rom. XI) I am herewith enclosing a letter of Fr. Edward's - rather a copy of Msgrs' that will speak for itself.

This passage presents a specific religious perspective on death and grieving.

The deceased person, Edwin, is believed to have transitioned from the temporary struggles of mortal life to a state of eternity. This afterlife is described as a destiny of confidence and union with one's highest ideals, free from the anxiety of earthly existence. It is believed that the deceased will receive a heavenly reward, based on the religious teaching that righteous and humble people are welcomed by God into a prepared state of joy.

For the person being addressed, who is now both an orphan and a widow, this loss is framed as having a specific meaning within a Christian faith context. The death of another loved one is viewed as a severing of one more tie that binds a person's heart to the earthly world.

Finally, the grieving person is offered the comfort that their deceased husband has joined their previously departed parents and other loved ones in the afterlife. The hope is expressed that all of these individuals now pray for, or watch over, the person who is still living.

If not this directly and fully, at least, please God, shortly to gain the crown and to hear the long hoped for greeting always awaiting the just and humble: "Come ye Blessed blessed of my Father possess to joys pre- pared for you ... The author expresses confidence that a divine remedy will be provided to compensate for the maternal, paternal, and spousal love that has been missing from the recipient's social and family life. The advice is to continue praying for guidance for oneself and for one's associates, with the assurance that God will provide direction toward the best outcome.

Regarding a choice between opportunities in Seattle and Los Angeles, the author favors the one in Seattle. This preference is especially strong if the daughters of a certain judge are old enough to be self-sufficient and manage their father's household. The author warns that in such situations, there is almost always a risk of jealousy. This kind of social difficulty is presented as a common part of life's struggles, which the author illustrates by paraphrasing a poem by Moore: people are driven through a troubled existence, and true calm can only be found in heaven.

Finally, the author states a refusal to comment on or become involved in the financial or business affairs that were mentioned.

Only just keep on praying for God's merciful guidance - for self and associates - and in His divine wisdom God will not fail you in His guidance for the best. Between the two outlooks in Seattle and Los Angeles, I am in- clined to favor that in the former. As for the financial or business affairs referred to, I just do not like to dabble into them.

The author, writing on a Holy Saturday in front of St. Felix Chapel, reflects on their religious conversion, a process they state has been ongoing since October 1870 and is still incomplete.

The central argument begins with a catechism question about the purpose of human existence: "Why did God make you?" The provided answer is, "God made me to know Him." This purpose is considered a blessed aim that also encompasses loving and serving God. For a grateful person, fulfilling this purpose is described as experiencing a foretaste of heaven while on Earth, and valuing this purpose correctly is said to be worth as much as heaven itself. The text asserts that loving God is the most rational action a person can take.

In contrast, the passage claims that atheism is the result of sin, which functions by suppressing a person's natural reason and gratitude. Atheism is strongly condemned and defined as the ultimate culmination of three things: intellectual insanity, moral degeneracy, and diabolical blasphemy.

The author expresses concern that the current era is a time when atheism, which is described as "the voice of Anti Christ," is demanding and receiving public attention. This situation is compared to the biblical event where the crowd chose to free Barabbas instead of Jesus, implying that society is making a similarly poor moral and spiritual choice by giving a platform to atheism.

The text also contains a personal wish for the well-being of a person named Margaret and her family.

At the time of the events described, the settlement of Prescot was very small, likely no larger than a village. A nearby location, Eagle Rock, was situated four miles downriver. To emphasize how undeveloped the area was, the author notes that even 15 years later, when they spent two weeks there with their Aunt Mary Ann, Eagle Rock was still so isolated it resembled a wilderness hermitage.

In this setting overlooking the Mississippi River (referred to as the "Father of Waters"), the author and four siblings were born.

The passage recounts a specific family hardship that occurred during the infancy of one of the siblings, a boy named Bernard. During Bernard's babyhood, the children's father contracted "the ague," an illness involving fever and chills, which caused him to go blind for two weeks. During this period, he had to be guided by hand. At the same time, his infant son and namesake, Bernard, suffered a rupture (a hernia). The author states that Bernard never fully recovered from this injury.

The author concludes by presenting a religious interpretation of these events. They express a firm belief that this trial, like all others, was part of God's plan. Looking back with gratitude, the author states with full conviction that "The Lord knows best" and offers praise for God's designs.

Here it was smiling down on the "Father of Waters", that five of us were privileged to breath our first morning air and "sing our first baby music", No doubt little Bernard must have been proficient in that music; because it was during his term of baby-hood that Papa went blind with the ague - when for two weeks he had to be led by the hand, and his little namesake got a rupture from which he never com- pletely recovered. A private road, known as "Lamb's Road," provided significant protection from these fires. This road was located on a ridge running east to west, approximately 30 rods (about 150 meters or 500 feet) to the south of the author's home. When the winds were not excessively strong, neighbors often had time to assist by lining up along the road to stop the fire from advancing across it.

This road's purpose was to provide access from the Miller farm, situated to the southwest, to a 20-acre field located to the southeast. A separate, public road passed directly by the author's residence, which was a one-story log cabin with dimensions of approximately 12 by 30 feet.

The house consisted of a single lower floor and a loft. The lower floor was divided by one partition to create a large bedroom area. The parents slept on one side of this partition, while their three daughters, Ellie, Maryann, and Mattie, slept on the other. The family's sons slept in the loft above, where they sometimes played in the mornings to the point of quarreling, which is described as typical behavior for boys.

The ceilings were low. While a person of average height could use the stairs without difficulty, a specific tall man named J.B. Fahey, who was 6 feet 2 inches, had to stoop to avoid hitting his head on the ceiling joists.

The house had a single entry door, located on the sunniest side of the building. For light, there was one window on each of the other two sides.

Winters in the area were harsh, and snow could accumulate as high as the peak of the gabled roof. Before the cold weather arrived, the father would insulate the base of the house by banking it with material. This preparation kept the family reasonably comfortable inside, regardless of strong winds or freezing temperatures.

On Sundays at 10:00 AM, the father would lead the family in reading Mass Prayers at home. However, when the weather was good and the roads were passable, he would walk about six miles, using shortcuts, to attend a physical church. On those occasions, other family members, such as Ellie or James, would lead the prayers at home. To the narrator, these prayer sessions sometimes seemed quite long.

The writer began this letter on the Feast of the Immaculate Conception, a date that also marked the 42nd anniversary of their religious vocation at St. Bonaventure's. They express gratitude to God and the Virgin Mary for this calling.

After being interrupted, the writer is now finishing the letter within the eight-day observance period (octave) following the feast. They state their motivation for writing is a feeling of gratitude for their vocation and religious order. This gratitude is particularly strong because they learned to love the order quickly, despite having been prejudiced against it and joining somewhat unwillingly.

The writer wishes the recipient well, hoping they are at least trying to be content. They report having prayed the rosary for the recipient's intentions and guidance that morning, outdoors in the crisp, moonlit air.

The writer concludes with an expression of confidence. They acknowledge that the recipient, like all human beings, faces difficulties, temptations, failures, and occasional small successes. Despite these common struggles, the writer believes that God will protect the recipient from making any serious mistakes.
styled: God bless you and I hope you are well -- trying at least to be contented. I started to write you on the beautiful Feast of our Blessed Mother, the Immaculate Conception; being as it was the 42nd anniversary of the happy day of my vocation to St. Bonaventure's. Thanks be to God and the same His Blessed Immaculate Mother. As often happens, however, I did not get far with my letter that day; so now, before the octave passes, I'll try once more. This I've wanted to do out of gratitude for such a vocation to such an order and, I might say, especially for the grace of learning so quickly to love the Order -- notwithstanding my prejudice on coming hither as I did, half against my will. I offered my rosary this morning out in the crisp, moon-light air for your intentions and your guidance. I am confident that though, like the rest of us -- poor children of Eve -- you have your difficulties, your temptations, your falls even, and your occasional little triumphs, our dear Lord will keep you from serious blunderings.

The author expresses a hope that the recipient will use their remaining years to work toward spiritual salvation. This goal is framed as the single most worthy achievement for a human being.

The author questions the assumption of having even a "few years," noting that the length of a person's life is subject to a divine will and that death could occur at any time. As a specific point of reference, living for another ten years would mean exceeding the typical age of their family members.

The letter stated that if one plan did not work out, the writer would become a lay-brother. The writer was determined never to live a purely secular life.

This letter was shown to Father Bonaventure, who was at that time a former Provincial and the Father Superior in Yonkers. He was pleased with the letter's contents, remarking that the writer had good intentions and should be encouraged to proceed.

In a later letter, the same person announced a return to college after a twenty-year absence. The college was located in Berlin, Ontario (now known as Kitchener). In this letter, the writer expressed a profound sense of peace, stating it was the peace they had been seeking for a long time. This feeling was described as sufficient compensation for the sacrifice of giving up everything to make this change.

This experience is presented as a practical example of the principle that a sacrifice made willingly for a spiritual purpose is always small when compared to the positive results that are sure to follow.

The recipient of the message and their brother, who is three years younger, share a long-held ambition to become missionaries. This raises several questions: when to begin, where their efforts would be most effective and appreciated, and whether they should travel to distant locations or focus their work closer to home, in line with the principle that charity begins locally.

The passage proposes that the most fundamental mission field is within one's own self. The central argument is that since any action taken for the salvation of one's own soul is entirely for the glory of God, extensive travel is not necessary for missionary work. Each individual has the primary and essential responsibility to save their own soul. The text emphasizes this point by stating that saving the entire world would be meaningless if a person failed to save their own soul.

The author concludes with a personal note expressing frustration with the quality of the writing, mentioning that it was frequently interrupted and that they would rewrite it if given more time. This is followed by an expression of thanks to God and a reflection on a shared human fallibility.

Shall we go to the ends of the earth, or shall we, convinced that Charity, rightly ordered, begins at home? Shall we begin right in our own hearts? The passage suggests that people frequently worry about numerous concerns, similar to the biblical figure Martha. In doing so, they often undervalue the principle of learning from a figure who is "meek and humble of heart." The biblical figure Mary the Penitent is presented as an example of someone who understood this concept and was praised by Jesus for it.

The text asserts a belief that if individuals were to fully accept and act on the divine assistance, or "graces," which are said to be continuously available to everyone, they could undergo a rapid and profound transformation from being a "great sinner" to a "great saint."

To support this idea, the passage includes a quote from a letter written by a once-prominent religious figure and author who has recently been experiencing a period of intense suffering. In the letter, this person expresses a state of complete humility and a sense of personal powerlessness. The writer states they have come to understand that they are nothing, possess nothing, and can achieve nothing on their own. All that remains is a very weak desire—a "tiny flicker of a weak will"—to simply *want* to persevere and remain faithful, whatever the personal cost. The writer also expresses the belief that God is saddened by their situation.

Finally, the text includes a logistical note, stating that a copy of a "rhyme-letter," which the recipient had given to a former provincial superior two years prior, is being enclosed.

The author of the passage expresses the following points in response to a letter they received:

The author acknowledges receiving a letter that contains an undertone of dissatisfaction. This dissatisfaction is described as understandable and not something for which the recipient is to be blamed.

Despite this, the author is very pleased with the letter because it displays a tone of patient resignation. This quality is considered to be of greater spiritual value than any of the recipient's past successes in their work, such as on missions, in parishes, or in teaching. The author views this patient resignation as both a result of and a catalyst for Christian humility.

The author proposes a theological interpretation of the recipient's current difficult circumstances. These challenges are framed as a divinely provided opportunity—a metaphorical "mill"—designed with wisdom and mercy to refine the recipient's character and develop the virtues that are considered most spiritually important.

It is seen as a very hopeful sign that the recipient, even in their present hardship, can still express the sentiment "Not to us, Lord, not to us..." (a phrase signifying that glory belongs to God, not to oneself). The author finds this especially significant given that the recipient has maintained this humility throughout a 33-year career in the priesthood, which is described as a difficult struggle containing both failures and successes.

The passage concludes with the central idea that gratitude should be directed primarily toward God and divine grace, followed by an expression of praise.
styled: God bless you and yours -- including my poor self I hope. I received your welcome letter yesterday and, while there is a silent note therein of dis- satisfaction, that I can hardly be surprized at or blame you for, yet I am more than pleased and I thank God for what, in my opinion, must please Heaven better than any success you ever had -- or could have without it -- on missions, parishes or catechism teachings. Thank God for your tone of patient resignation, at once a great promoter and a fruit of Christian humility. God himself has provide in your present trying circumstances, a mill in His wisdom and in His mercy for your refinement in these virtues that pleas Him most. It seems to me a most hopeful indication if, notwithstanding your blunders as well as your successes for three and thirty years in the holy Priesthood -- in the brunt of the warfare, therefore -- and especially under your present trying circumstances, you can still sigh: "Non nobis Domine! non nobis ... ". Its God and His holy grace more than anything else that we ought thak. Blessed be His Holy Name!

A well-known priest, lecturer, and writer from Ironton, Ohio, named Father Cotter, recently recounted a story from his 50th anniversary as a priest. After receiving a great deal of praise for his long service, he spoke with his sister, who remarked that the most important thing to be thankful for was that he had managed to avoid any major scandal during those 50 years.

The lesson from this anecdote is that one should be grateful for everything, including both difficult experiences and positive ones.

Based on this principle, one should not judge the Father Chaplain too harshly, even if he seems overly demanding. His position is likely stressful and probably requires him to handle sensitive and difficult cases from time to time.

Instead of finding fault, it is better to be supportive of the Chaplain and everyone else associated with the institution. All of them face their own challenges and have personal flaws. Consequently, trying to assign blame is not a productive exercise.

How we ought to thank God that for these fifty years He has never per- mitted you to/any real scandal." So dear Brother, Fr. Joachim: let us be grateful to God for everything -- the knocks we get as well as the consolations. ... and do not blame the Father Chaplain too severely if he seem unduly exacting, etc. Of all positions he has one that in my opinion must at times be on his nerves. A divine institution like the Church could have been established under the leadership of flawless, superhuman beings. However, it is instead composed of and managed by imperfect people. The fact that this institution endures despite the inherent flaws of its human members is presented as a remarkable, even miraculous, achievement. This same principle can be extended to most charitable organizations, which are also run by imperfect individuals.

Given this reality, an individual's role and privilege is to contribute through small, seemingly insignificant actions. The passage argues that large, high-profile tasks are less important for an individual to focus on, as there will always be people willing to take on these roles, even if they sometimes fail significantly.

In contrast, there is a special value in performing the small, mundane, and often unnoticed tasks. The significance of these simple actions—such as cleaning, manual labor, enduring minor personal hardships, offering brief prayers, or expressing sympathy—is profound and can be appreciated on a higher, spiritual level.

This emphasis on small deeds is supported by the idea that an accumulation of minor actions leads to perfection, and perfection itself is a significant and divine quality. The passage concludes that from a divine perspective, the entire world is fundamentally composed of these small, individual components.

The central advice of the passage is to refrain from blaming a person referred to as "Father Chaplain" for seeming overly demanding or strict. His strictness is presented as evidence of his conscientiousness, as a less dedicated priest would likely not hold such a difficult and trying position, which involves handling sensitive issues.

To support this point, an anecdote is shared about Father Cotter, a well-known priest, writer, and lecturer from Ironton, Ohio. At the celebration of his 50th year in the priesthood, after receiving a great deal of praise, his respected sister commented that the most significant cause for thankfulness was that God had prevented him from causing any major scandal during those five decades. The intent of this story is to frame the avoidance of serious moral failure as a priest's greatest achievement and to attribute that success to divine help, not personal merit. This reinforces the idea that glory should be given to God, not to individuals.

The passage suggests that instead of finding fault, one should pray for the chaplain and for everyone else involved in the institution. It makes the claim that all of them face their own challenges and have personal flaws.

The final argument is a theological one: God established the Church to be run by imperfect human beings, not by flawless angels. Consequently, one should expect and tolerate human faults and weaknesses in all people, including those in positions of authority, rather than assigning blame.

The writer began this communication at 11 p.m. following a day that was busy and eventful for them. They acknowledge, however, that the day was undoubtedly more eventful for the recipient and others directly experiencing the Eucharistic Congress in the Philippines.

From their location in Detroit, the writer and others listened to radio announcements about the Congress at approximately 8 a.m. local time. They were able to hear a broadcast of the Pope's voice delivering a blessing, which the writer believes concluded with the Latin words, "...in Nomine Patris et Filii et Spiritus Sancti."

The writer requests that the recipient share significant details about the event, explaining that the press coverage in their area, including Catholic media, has been surprisingly minimal.

Finally, the writer expresses a hope that the Philippine Congress was even more solemn and impressive than a previous one held in Ireland. To convey the high standard of the Irish event, the writer notes that Cardinal Hayes was said to have described it as having "surpassed the insurpassible."
styled: God bless you . I hope you are well - you and yours. Though it is just striking 11 p.m. I want to at least start you a few words before re- tiring after this busy day, and in a way even for me eventful day. For yourself of course, and for every one whose privilege it has been to be in immediate touch with the Eucharistic Congress out there in the Philippines it has been no doubt more than eventful. However, we here get the announce- ments over the radeo about 8 a.m. in Detroit and heard the Holy Father's own voice and benediction. His conclusion with benediction seemed to be really: ". in Nomine Patris et Filii et Spiritus Sancti". I hope you may send us details worth while. The press here - even the Catholic part of it has been very tame so far about this great event. I hope to learn that it surpassed in solemnity and impressiveness even the grandeur, etc, of the Congress in Ireland, of which Cardinal Hayes is said to have remarked: "It surpassed the insurpassible".

This is a delayed account of a journey. The trip was authorized several months in advance by the Reverend Father Provincial after being discussed with Father M. Joachim.

The author's journey began on the evening of Wednesday, June 3rd. The weather was clear, with a visible sunset and moonlight. The group crossed the Niagara River approximately 13 miles upstream from the Falls, where the author observed that the water's current was powerful and turbulent.

Despite sleeping very little overnight, the author was not tired. By dawn, their transport was traveling down the Mohawk Valley, making only one or two stops before Albany. From there, the journey continued south along the Hudson River to Garrison, which is located across the river from the West Point Military Academy.

Upon arrival, the author walked about one mile to a monastery and conducted a Mass at approximately 9:00 a.m. Finding the location very appealing, the author decided to stay for an extra day to rest.

The monastery grounds are described as extremely spacious and impressively grand. The author believes the property was originally over 400 acres in size.
styled: Hoping that it may not be without interest, I'll try just briefly to give you an idea about the whole affair even though be- lated. Father M. Joachim seems to have spoken to Rev. Father Provincial about it some months before, and the latter told me it would be alright. I started off Wednesday evening June 3rd. The evening and night were ideal in sun-set and moon-light, we crossed the Niagara about 13 miles above the Falls but even at that the waters seemed to be swirling on to as if rushing to a tragedy. Though I slept very little I was not tired when the dawn re- vealed we were descending the Mchawk Valley stopping only once or twice before reaching Albany. Then down the Hudson to Garrison just across from Westpoint Military Academy. Walking to the Monastery about a mile below, I said holy Mass close to 9 a.m. Deo Gratias! I found things so inviting afterwords that I decided to rest there a day. The grounds are spacious to say the least and I might say almost dangerously grand. Originally there were, I believe over 400 acres.

They believe they might have been sent to the 1937 event if it had occurred closer in time to the recipient's jubilee. However, the writer was not otherwise seeking to make such an expensive and unusual trip unless it was required by an official duty.

Instead, the writer was sent to New York the previous June to assist a person named Father Maurice with a celebration. This trip seemed appropriate at the time, and in retrospect, the writer considers it to have been a fortunate and beneficial experience for themself and for others. As an example of these benefits, the writer intends to enclose a letter from Mary Kerrman, a patient at St. Elizabeth Hospital in Elizabeth, New Jersey, who is described as an "ascetic invalid."

The writer acknowledges that the recipient was expecting a report about this ten-day trip to New York and had asked for details about a major Congress. They explain that they have made several unsuccessful attempts to write a summary of the visit. The writer also advises the recipient not to use their personal experience as the standard by which to judge the entire Congress.

I have not been anxious, however, to under- take such an expensive and extraordinary trip, - unless of course some ad- ditional duty should waft me thither. The writer recounts two challenging descents.

First, the writer made a descent on what was believed to be a completely unexplored route. The writer was aided by a sturdy staff and was motivated by memories of similar, though smaller, climbs from 60 or more years in the past. The journey involved some narrow escapes, and a vehicle's rear fenders sustained a few harmless bumps. The writer expresses a sense of gratitude for having completed the descent safely. Arriving back at a monastery around dinnertime, the writer had a strong appetite. That evening included a happy recreational period, after which the writer slept exceptionally well.

The next day, a person identified as Father Guardian, who had business in New York, drove the writer by car. Their route passed between the landmarks of Sugar-loaf and Mount of Atonement and descended through the High-lands region. This descent was also very steep. After driving down so many hills that the writer began to assume they were nearing level ground, they passed a sign that simply read "Hill." The writer found this amusing. The driver, who appeared to know every detail of the road, drove swiftly over that hill and continued to navigate a series of further inclines.
styled: I think it was a totally unexplored route; but aided by a strong emergency staff, and dreamings of similar climb- ings - though on smaller scales - 60 or more years ago, I made the descent with some narow escapes and a few harmless bumps on rear fenders. Deo Gratias. It was close to supper-time when I got back to the monastery, and I need not tell you I had an appetite. We had recreation that evening which ... very happy and its a long time since I slept sounder than that night. Next day, finding he had some extra business in New York, Fr. Guardian brought me down by auto. We crossed over between Sugar-loaf and the now famous Mt. of Atonement and went down over the High-lands. It was quite a descent indeed. After we had gone down so many hills that I was beginning to think we were coming close to normally level ground we suddenly curved past a sign: "Hill". I had to smile as we dashed past it and over the top, the dri- ver seemingly knowing every inch and bump ahead till again and again we con- tinued to make inclines.

The simple act of reading a book does not, by itself, cause a divine being to grant a favor. Reading is only effective in this regard when the text helps to elevate a person's thoughts and emotions toward the divine. It is through this process of spiritual elevation that the reading takes on the qualities of a prayer, which in turn can attract divine blessings.

Furthermore, for a person to gain any spiritual benefit from reading—even from sacred texts or prayers about God—the reader must have the correct internal disposition. To profit from reading about spiritual matters, one must approach the text with an attitude of reverence and appreciation.
styled: But where the connection between reading a book and the obtain- ing of such a favor! Why urge such reading? Why suggest it as a last remedy when everything else seems futle? This might seem quite a question to ask. And as a rule questions are more easily asked than answered. It ought to be selfunderstood that no simple reading of any book is going to move the Heart of Heaven in our favor. Only inasmuch as any book or page can serve to raise the heart to God and thus draw His blessings to us can it be said to have any quality of prayer a- bout it. But besides this, to profit by reading, even the holyist prayers - even about God Himself - the heart of the reader must be disposed. In other words if we want to profit by our reading about God and His saints we must read with reverence. We must appreciate.

A man, who was thought to be very distressed by repeated disappointments in the East, traveled west. This was confirmed by a second message from Baltimore that arrived less than a week after a previous one.

In Baltimore, this man went to St. Agnes Hospital to be treated for a carbuncle. After his treatment, he asked hospital staff to take him to the B. & O. Railroad Depot to travel to Chicago. However, the staff, believing he was in no condition to travel by himself, sent him to a retreat instead.

The author of the passage believes the hospital staff acted with good intentions and considers this outcome to have been very fortunate or divinely arranged. Upon learning more about the retreat and reflecting on the man's condition, the author became even more convinced that it was the best possible place for him. The author and others at a monastery viewed the man being sent to the retreat as an answer to their prayers and as evidence of divine guidance.

Later, the author realized a possible connection between this outcome and an earlier suggestion they had made: to actively pray a text called "the Coronation" rather than to just read it.
styled: Heart-sick, as I imagine he must have been, at disa- pointment after disapointment, in the East, he had turned his steps again westward, as a second communication from Baltimore indicated hardly a week after the former. In Baltimore he had gone to St. Agnes Hospital for treatment on his carbuncle and had afterwards requested the authorities to get him to the B. & O. Depot for Chicago. Instead, however, they had sent him out to said retreat, conscientiously no doubt - providentially I trust - convinced that he was in no fit condition to be traveling a- lone. Indeed the more we have learned about that institution and the more I've considered his condition both at the time and since, the more too am I convinced that he could hardly landed in a better or a more providential place. At all events we at the Monastery here looked opon his going thither as an answer to prayer and as an evi- dence that he was in God's guidance. Only later on it dawned on my mind that my simple proposition - as said above - to pray, rather than simply read, the "Coronation".

A man named Maurice had to leave the seminary due to poor health. This outcome was a disappointment to his family, and Maurice described himself as "a misfit, a personal failure." His father, who often used the proverb "Man proposes, God disposes" to explain events, would sigh and express a wish that he had become a priest himself. The stress of this period was also evident in Maurice's mother, whose hair began to turn gray.

After many years passed, it is noted that the circumstances were naturally discouraging for Maurice. The passage states that this was one of many hardships he had faced and would continue to face, referencing the belief that God tests those who are loved.

Eventually, Maurice adjusted to his situation. He decided that the next best course of action was to encourage others to pursue religious vocations. In this way, he hoped to inspire someone else to take the place he was unable to fill as a priest, serving at the altar, in the confessional, and on missions.
styled: Alas! however, as dear Father was wont to repeat, the proverb: "Man proposes-God disposes." Poor, dear Maurice's health failed and he came home from the Seminary a family disappointment and worse than that in his own words: "a misfit, a personal failure - - a sadly misfit and personal failure." Ah! It was about that time that silver began to tell its story in Mother's hair and Father's sighs would bring a gentle Soliloquy: "If I had to start life over again, I'd be a priest." . . Winters and summers slipped away. Years and decacs rolled by. Never to be discouraged under such circumstances would surely be more than human. But this was by no means the first knock he had met, and God, if "those whom God loves He tries," it was far from being the last he was to wether. It did not take too long to adjust himself to what seemed next best. He would promote vocations in others at least and in this way possibly in- fluence someone to take his place at the Altar, in the confessional, on the missions.

The author expresses hope that the recipient is well and speculates that the recipient's lack of communication is due to being busy, a situation the author also experiences. The author feels that time is passing very quickly, leading to a sense of pressure and a feeling of not accomplishing enough. As an example, the author has a large backlog of letters they feel obligated to write but are unable to send, despite wanting to and knowing that replies are expected.

Regarding health, the author reports being in good health, which is attributed to God. They state that they regularly work up to 18 hours a day without feeling weighed down. The monastery community has also been healthy this year, with very few colds or other sicknesses. The author expresses a wish that the community will become more appreciative of what they consider to be divine graces.

Finally, the author conveys good news about Father Joachim, for which they also express gratitude to God. An enclosed copy of a letter from Father Joachim will show that he anticipates being able to celebrate Mass again soon.
styled: God bless you and yours. I hope you are well and that the silence you maintain is only an indication that your time, like my own, flies, whither I hardly know; so that it seems almost continually blaming me for doing nothing and getting nowhere. There are so many letters, e. g. I ought to write and still so few I get off, as I would like to do personally, and as is often expected. Thanks be to God, however, my health has been good; so that, as a rule 18 hours a day hardly seems to weigh me down at all. Again, "Deo Gratias." We've had hardly any colds in the Monastery this year and very little sickness otherwise. I just hope that we may some day learn to appreciate His graces and be grateful to God. Thanks be to God, we have good word from Father Joachim, as the en- closed copy of his letter will convince you. According to it, you will see that he is figuring on saying Holy Mass again before long.

A man named Father M.J. has undergone a significant negative change, described as a "defection," which has been a concern for nearly two years. The problem first became apparent through a period of noticeable and troubling restlessness. Both the author of the passage and its recipient attempted to intervene by offering him sincere, practical advice in writing. Despite these efforts, several months passed before a more definitive break occurred.

The precise cause and nature of Father M.J.'s mental state are difficult to determine. For some time, he had been suffering from a severe carbuncle on the back of his neck. It is unclear whether this painful physical ailment was a cause of his mental distress, a symptom of another underlying issue, or unrelated. The condition was severe enough that it could have plausibly affected his mental stability.

A local doctor examined him but found no conclusive evidence of a mental disorder. Nevertheless, the people at the monastery felt they were unable to care for him or manage his condition. As a result, they sent him to a hospital, possibly in Fond du Lac, Wisconsin. At the hospital, the prevailing belief was that he was suffering from cerebral arteriosclerosis (hardening of the arteries in the brain) or a similar condition.
styled: God grant it may come to that soon -- "Deo Volente." I am not sure if I told you before of my dismay at same poor, dear Fr. M. J. 's defection, as it has seemed now close to two years, viz., since his unrest began to show itself threatening. You wrote him at the time yourself, earnest, practical lines of advice. I tried to do so too. Well, months went on before the real break came. What was in his mind, and how it was there, is not easy to say. He had been suffering for quite some time from a fearful carbuncle on the back of his neck - whether a cause or an effect of something else - enough to set many a man crazy. At all events, while the local doctor found nothing positively wrong with his mind, there seemed to be little or nothing to be done for him or with him in the Monastery. They sent him, there- fore, to the hospital in Fond du Lac, Wis., or some other, where his case was believed to be hardening of the brain-arteries or something of that nature.

Instead of rushing to complete the book, the writer decided to start again from the beginning with the intention of reading it with proper reverence. This presented a problem, as the priest's previous attempts to gain admission to the hospital had been unsuccessful.

A man, identified as Father M.J., returned to the Monastery and apologized to the Father Provincial for any scandal he had caused. This was followed by a conference that was reportedly difficult and not friendly.

Afterward, having received his official letter of departure, he took a flight to Chicago. The general assumption among his peers was that he was en route to his home diocese, likely via St. Paul. The author of the passage, however, privately thought he might travel to the West Coast before returning to his diocese.

The author felt great concern because Father M.J.'s behavior seemed uncharacteristic. The author could only respond with hope and prayer, drawing a parallel to how a "saintly Mother" must have felt 55 years prior when Father M.J. had a breakdown at the seminary and had to come home.

Consequently, the author was surprised to receive a telegram a few days later from the Rector of St. Mary's Seminary in Baltimore, Maryland. The message stated that Father M.J. had arrived there and was not well. In a phone call that night, the author learned further details: Father M.J. had managed to celebrate Mass once or twice, but with difficulty, and had since traveled on to New York.

For any written work to have a prayer-like quality, it must be capable of elevating a person's thoughts to God and thereby attracting divine blessings.

To gain spiritual benefit from reading, even from the most sacred texts about God, the reader must approach the material with the correct internal disposition. This means that a person must read with a sense of reverence and appreciation.

As an example, texts such as the Bible and the Gospels are considered "holy" for two reasons. First, the Church has declared them to be divinely inspired writings. Second, millions of people have historically benefited from reading them devoutly, which has led them to believe in and love God.

However, not everyone who reads these same sacred texts benefits. Some gain nothing, while for others, the experience is actively harmful. The reason for this difference in outcomes is a failure in the reader's disposition and a lack of reverence.

The passage concludes by citing a scriptural concept that people who are "unlearned and unstable" misinterpret or distort the scriptures, which leads to their own spiritual destruction.
styled: Only inas- much as any book or page can serve to raise the heart to God and thus draw His blessings to us can it be said to have any quality of prayer about it. But, besides this, to profit by reading, even the holiest prayers - even about God Himself - the heart of the reader must be disposed. In other words, if we want to profit by our reading about God and his saints, we must read with reverence. We must appreciate. We speak of the Holy Bible, the Holy Gospel, etc., because the Church has declared them to be inspired writings and because millions have profited from their perusal; have learned to believe in God and to love Him by devoutly reading about Him therein. Others have read the same holy pages without profit; others again, to their own detriment. Why so? How? Failure of disposition; Want of reverence. "Unlearned and unstable wresting the scriptures to their own destruction.
