A person’s placement in a particular institution is regarded, with the benefit of hindsight and greater knowledge, as the most favorable and fortunate outcome that could have occurred. The community at a monastery viewed this event as an answer to prayer and as clear evidence of divine guidance, considering it a cause for gratitude.

Subsequently, the idea emerged that a specific suggestion—to actively pray rather than to simply read a book titled "Coronation"—might also have been a factor in this positive result. This prompts an inquiry into the connection between reading a book and receiving such a favorable intervention. The passage questions why reading would be urged as a last resort when all other methods have failed.

It concludes with the principle that the mechanical act of reading a book is not, in itself, sufficient to bring about divine favor.
styled: Indeed, the more we have learned about that in- stitution and the more I've considered his condition, both at the time and since, the more too am I convinced that he could hardly have landed in a better or a more providential place. Deo Gratias At all events, we at the Monastery here looked upon his going thither as an answer to prayer and as nothing less than evidence that he was in God's guidance. Only later, it dawned on my mind that my simple proposition -- as said above -- to pray, rather than simply read the "Coronation" was, possibly, being considered too. But where the connection between reading a book and the obtain- ing of such a favor? Why urge such reading? Why suggest it as a last remedy when everything else seems futile? This might seem quite a question to ask, and, as a rule, questions are more easily asked than answered. Several points are presented to support this claim and to validate the human writer's sincerity and modesty:

*   **Institutional Approval:** The work has received strong and repeated endorsement from Catholic universities, bishops, and popes, despite facing opposition.
*   **Intrinsic Quality and Harmony:** It possesses inherent value and is in clear alignment with the Bible, philosophy, and sacred theology. The passage asserts that the work is not merely compatible with these fields but holds a position of outstanding superiority in relation to them.
*   **Spiritual Significance:** It is recognized as a pinnacle achievement within the practice of asceticism.

The passage concludes that these factors should be sufficient to convince an honest person of the writer's central claim: that the work's true author is Mary, who is described with titles such as the master of heavenly wisdom, the Queen of the Universe, the Virgin Mother of God, and one conceived without sin.

A man known as Gus preferred to be called Austin. The author of the source passage approved of this preference, noting its similarity to the name of a significant figure in Church history.

The author seeks more details about Austin's final days. Before his death, Austin wrote a letter from the hospital after undergoing his first surgery. He was aware he had cancer, and his letter was described as touching, calm, and philosophical about his prognosis, while also demonstrating strong religious faith.

In the letter, Austin made the following points:
*   He observed that cancer is seldom cured by surgery.
*   He stated his reliance on his faith in the "Sacred Heart" for help.
*   He reported receiving Holy Communion at 6 a.m. on the morning of his surgery and again on the second day following the procedure, a First Friday, for which he expressed gratitude.

The author notes that Austin died on the Feast of the Sacred Heart. The author interprets this timing as a merciful, divinely arranged "rescue."

Additionally, the author reports that even before his illness, Austin had frequently asked for prayers for a person named Pat. The author is certain that Austin was praying for a reconciliation with this person and believes that this reconciliation did occur, viewing it as a positive outcome.
styled: Gus - Austin rather, since he prefered and as I told him, so much more like the real name of the great doctor of the Church. I would like to have details of his last days. He wrote me quite a touching letter from the hospital apparently after his first operation, seemingly quite cool and philosophical about what might come -- and certainly with beautiful faith. He evidently knew that he had cancer. Just a few of his words: "I have observed that very seldom is cancer cured ... at least by surgery. "I am relying on the Sacred Heart to come to my rescue . " . .. "I was privileged to receive our Lord at 6 a.m. the morning they opened me; and again on the 2nd day (1st Friday) , Thanks and praise to the Sacred Heart." How beautifully condescending that the Merciful Sacred H't actually did come to his rescue on His own blessed Feast! He had written me a number of times to pray for Pat., even before he was sick. I am sure he was praying for his -- their reconsiliation, etc. and how beautifully did it not come about!

The author is concluding a note that was started on the evening of the 4th. An enclosed letter from a Miss Ryan in New York is intended to illustrate the author's ongoing hope of converting their family and relatives. The method for this conversion is to have them read and pray a book titled "The Mystical City of God," which is also referred to as the "Autobiography of God's eternally chosen Queen of the Universe."

The recipient, identified as Edward, is advised to write a line of appreciation and encouragement to Miss Ryan, with the suggestion that sending a verse would be even better.

Background information is provided about Miss Ryan and the book's history. Miss Ryan was a successful businesswoman before the war. Around 1942, a government order from Washington required that all printing plates ("prints and cuts") not in active use be destroyed unless a redemption fee was paid. The fee to save the plates for "The Mystical City of God" was approximately $500. The situation became difficult because a bishop, in whose jurisdiction the plates were stored, forbade their rescue. The passage notes that Miss Ryan has a special devotion to the Holy Ghost, implying her involvement in this situation.

The inclosed letter from Miss Ryan in New York will give an idea of what my hopes were -- still are -- of converting our wayward family and clan to seraphic love of God and our Bl. Mother Mary, by having them read and pray the wonderful, all-outstanding "Autobiography of God's eternally chosen Queen of the Universe", the "Mystical City of God". Dear Edward: I think Miss Ryan would appreciate a line from you, of appreciation and of encouragement. Better a verse. She had been quite a successful business-lady before the War. I think it was in 1942 that quite an unexpected order came from Washington to "scrap" all prints and cuts not in actual use unless redeemed, etc. The redemption-fee on the Mystical City of God prints was quite an item; $500.00 I believe; and with a bishop in whose jurisdiction these prints were stored forbidding the rescue, it certainly looked dark for them. However, Miss R. who seems to be specially devoted to the Holy Ghost ...

Based on the passage, the author expresses a confident hope that their deceased family members have achieved salvation and are in heaven.

This belief is held for another recently deceased person from their original family of sixteen, who joins the author's deceased mother and father. The author presents the following points:

*   **An Example for the Living:** The deceased are seen as encouraging those still alive to follow their example. This example consists of three main actions:
    1.  Maintaining religious faith.
    2.  Praying for one another, which is framed as a core religious duty ("Interests of the Sacred Heart").
    3.  Actively resisting temptation (described as "the world, the flesh and the devil").

*   **The Ultimate Goal:** The purpose of living this way is to achieve the ultimate reward of salvation, which is defined as the "Beatific Vision," or experiencing the direct presence of God after death. The author asserts that saving one's soul is the "one thing necessary" in life.

*   **Evidence for Hope:** This confidence in their salvation is based on several observations:
    *   The first two to die, Mary Ann and Martha, were innocent children.
    *   The others who died showed patience during their final struggles and appeared to have a strong faith in God.

*   **The Communion of Saints:** The author believes these deceased family members have joined a larger community of departed relatives and neighbors. This community of the dead and the living is interconnected through prayer; the dead are believed to pray for the living, and the living are encouraged to pray for the dead. The author identifies this entire dynamic as a real-world example of the theological doctrine of the "Communion of the Saints."

The author's intent is to express profound gratitude and praise to God for this comforting belief system and the hope it provides.
styled: How grateful we ought to be that we can confidently hope that we have another, another of our original sixteen -- with dear Father and Mother -- waving us from beyond the grave to follow their footsteps in keeping the faith, in praying for one another as among the INTERESTS OF THE SACRED HEART and striving manfully against the world, the flesh and the devil for the one great prize of the final BEATIFIC VISION. Mary Ann was the first to cross the border into eternity and saintly little Martha a week later -- innocent children -- and the others following after, judging from their patience in their final struggles and the seemingly brightness of their faith in God, give great hope that so far every one of them have made the Great Grade, have saved their souls -- the one thing necessary -- and with so many of our dear ones of kin and neighbors are praying for us and asking our prayers. Ah !.. What else is this than just a little side-view of the great Communion of the Saints? Thanks and praises and Glory be to God!

There is positive news regarding Father M. Joachim. The writer recently received a very cheerful letter from him, describing it as the best in a long time. The letter suggests that Father M. Joachim has returned to his former, more characteristic self, a development that brings the writer great relief.

The main subject concerns a proposed trip. The writer reminds the recipient of a letter sent to Father M. Joachim several weeks prior, which the writer believes was also copied to the recipient. This previous letter confirmed that the writer had already obtained permission for a trip to Chicago and St. Paul, with flexible timing. The writer had delegated the planning and arrangements for this trip to the recipient and Father M. Joachim.

A new development is the potential to add another destination. The Very Reverend Father Provincial, who has just returned from Guam and other Pacific islands, is expected to visit from Detroit soon. The writer plans to ask him for permission to also travel to Superior, as suggested by Father M. Joachim, and anticipates no difficulty in getting this approval.

The writer expects to have about a week available for the entire trip and is asking for any suggestions that might make the travel proposition more interesting.
styled: I hope this finds you in the best of health and hopes. Thanks be to God we are quite well down here in St. Felix. After a cold and wet spring -- even black frost on the 8th the weather has turned quite ideal. Deo Gr. I was certainly pleased to receive a very bright letter from Fr. M. Joachim last week, about the best in a long time. It really looks like his old self once more. Thanks be to God "a billion." I wrote him several weeks ago that I had already permis - sion to go on a trip to Chicago and St. Paul, etc. at my choice and leaving the arrangements to yourself and him. I believe he said he sent you a copy of said letter. Well, We expect V. Rev. Fr. Provincial down from Detroit shortly -- just back from Guam and several other islands in the Pacific, and I anticipate no difficulty in obtaining permission to go also to Superior as M. J. proposes. I would be glad to have any suggestions that might heighten interests relative to the proposition. I'll probably get a week or so off for the trip.

The information below is a summary of a text written by Monsignor Edward F. Casey.

**Author and Family Details**
The author wrote the original text to his youngest brother, who is about fifteen months younger than him. The author is concerned about their second-oldest brother, Father M. J., who is now the eldest living brother in the family.

The family had thirteen children in total: ten sons and three daughters. A brother named Owen was the youngest of the ten sons. The three sisters are still living and are now grandmothers.

**The Mother's Death**
The author mentions his mother's death, describing it in positive terms. He expresses the religious belief that her death was a "wonderful victory" and a "Happy Death," and hopes she is now in heaven. He is grateful to God for providing her with what he calls "great grace" during a ten-day period preceding her death, which he characterizes as a "fearful, yet glorious struggle."

**Author's Wartime Experience**
A postscript notes that the author, Monsignor Edward Casey, was a prisoner in a Japanese prison camp called "Los Bonos." He was one of more than 2,000 prisoners who were rescued. Among the other prisoners were two bishops, 150 priests, and 125 nuns.

The rescue was conducted by forces under General MacArthur early in the morning on February 23, 1943. The author states that this was the day the prisoners believed their Japanese captors were planning to massacre them.

Owen was the youngest of ten brothers with three sister among his nine brothers ahead of him and three more immediately following. These three are still living -- now grandmas. The writer briefly touches on dear Mother's beautiful death. May she rest with saints in Heaven. Thanks be to God for the great grace He provided her, for the ten-day fearful, yet glorious struggle, that preceeded her wonderful victory in a Happy Death P. S. The writer of the above, Rt. Rev. Edw'd, was rescued from the Jap. Prison Los Bonos. with two bishops, 150 priest and one hundred twenty-five nuns among over 2000 prisoners. Very early the morning of February 23rd, 1943 the day on which the desperate Japps would seem to have been planing a whole-sale masacre of them; they were rescued by the MacArthur Forces.

A religious superior, the Guardian, has tentatively suggested that the writer could begin a new assignment on June 1st or 2nd. The writer considers this to be too early unless there is a specific reason for it. The start date could be flexible, for instance, to accommodate a mission assignment that might take place before or, preferably, after an upcoming anniversary.

Currently, a leadership group called the Definitorium is meeting for several days at Saint Bonaventure's. The writer understands that immediately after this meeting, the Father Provincial, who has recently completed extensive travel, intends to come to the writer's location for a rest, which the writer presumes will be a private retreat.

There is a possibility the writer could be transferred to Detroit or elsewhere, but this is considered highly unlikely. The writer is unconcerned about the outcome, viewing a transfer and staying in the current location as essentially the same. This indifference is based on the belief that the greatest privilege is knowing with certainty that one is following God's will by obeying superiors and adhering to the rules of the order.

The writer concludes with the reflection that the members of their community, including the writer, do not fully appreciate this privilege of obedience.
styled: Rev. Fr. Guardian, after a little consultation just noted -- tentatively -- that I could start June 1st or 2nd. Of course I think that would be rather early, unless there were a purpose for it. If we had a mission to do somewhere before the anniversary or possibly preferably after, we could arrange accordingly. They are having a meeting in Saint Bonaventure's these three or four days, of the Definitorium and I understand that right thereafter Father Provincial after many thousand miles travel is figuring on coming down here for a rest. -- a sort of private retreat for himself I presume. There is a possibility that I be sent back there to Detroit or elsewhere, though I hardly think it at all probable. I have not the least worry about whether I re- main here or be transferred. It is after all, essentially quite the same. It is such a surpassing privilege to know definitely that one is doing God's holy will by keeping the rule and obeying. Sorry to say, if we can use the word, it is so little possible for any of us to appreciate such privileges.

A telegram arrived two nights ago, and a person named Grace telephoned yesterday morning to provide more details and ask that this information be shared.

Bernard, Sr. required hospital treatment for a medical issue. The problem arose on Thursday evening while he was in Eureka for business. He was occupied and delayed responding to a physical need, which led to the complication. According to Grace, the condition is not considered to be comparatively serious. It is hoped that the situation is indeed not serious, and it is considered wise to be concerned that no significant complications result from such an event.

The writer and their household are reportedly in good health. They have experienced a very mild winter with very little snow and a low incidence of common colds. This has occurred despite significant rainfall. Early in the week, there was an episode of sleet and freezing rain that was heavy enough in some locations to weigh down the branches of trees and shrubs to the point of breaking.

We've had a very mild Winter, hardly any snow to speak of and practically no colds. All this, not- withstanding quite a lot of rain and early in the week a visita- tion of sleet and freezing rain that in quite a few places shrubs and trees were loaded down to breaking down. The inclosed telegram came the night before last and Grace phoned yesterday morning giving more particulars and asking that I let you know about the situation. Bernard, Sr. had been out on some official busines in Eureka, was quite occupied Thursday evening so that he neglected some kind of a natural call to which he was not as promptly obedient as Grandmother Nature often has to insist on. I've not said holy Mass since last Thursday. The skin-burns I wrote you about last week (if it got off), started the eczema activity again - after I'd had a Dr. Stan Casey treat the former. He sent me to a skin- specialist in Ft. Wayne, Dr. McNairy, who stresses with treatment, "feet up." I would have offered holy Mass yesterday but Fr. Guardian thought better keep to Dr.'s orders. So that will probably mean a week or so before I'm on my feet again properly. Thanks be to God is gives me comparatively little pain or itch; so that time does not hang so painfully as it might otherwise. Extremely brief of course, but even so, who knows how many a vocation its simple reading may be destined to awaken, to encourage, to anchor. Ah ! "Its simple reading' ?

The purpose of this writing would be twofold: first, to examine the events as a demonstration of what they considered to be divine providence, and second, to express their gratitude to the many people, both old and new friends, who had shown them kindness.

The author states that it is unnecessary to include details about the early preparations for the celebration. This is because the intended recipient of the message is already aware of them. The recipient is the most senior member of the family since the death of a person named Ella and has followed the lives of the family members for a longer time and with more interest than anyone else alive.

This familiarity with the family's history is also true, though to a lesser extent, for other relatives. These include "Brother Pat," Guss, and Owen. It also applies to Margaret, Grace, and Mayme, who were once called "the three little sisters" but are now old enough to be grandmothers. Their perspective on the family's earliest years is naturally more limited than the recipient's.

The author concludes by noting an uncertainty about whether they had ever previously written to the recipient about an individual referred to as "Fr."
styled: Musing together over the celebration of his Jubilee, and the triple vacation it occasioned us, we agreed that it were theme enough for a little treatise of some kind, whereby to praise the wonderful ways of God's providence, and at the same time, offer an expression of appreciation to the many dear ones -- old and new -- and for the gratitude we all experienced at so many manifestations of kindness at their hands. Details of preparations for that celebration, at least the more remote, will hardly be necessary or expected here. As the Senior of the family -- since dear Ella passed away -- you know those details; having watched the career of each of us longer and perhaps with more interest than anyone else breathing to- day. Something the same might be said also to poor, dear Brother Pat, and, for that matter, though of course with shorter scope of vision back to earlier spring-time of life, to each of the others -- Guss and Owen, and the one-time three little sisters -- now we might say Grandmas -- Margaret, Grace and Mayme. I am not certain if I ever wrote you of Fr.

The author of the passage was sent to New York to help with the celebration, which lasted for a week to ten days and was considered very pleasant.

This visit occurred approximately 12 years after the author had completed a 20-year period of living in New York State. In the roughly seven years he had been there, Father Maurice Joachim had become well-acquainted with people in the same three posts where the author had previously been assigned.

The high point of the Jubilee was a solemn Mass, which proceeded successfully. A number of relatives, including two nuns, traveled from Boston and other areas to attend. In the days that followed, the author and others visited their organization's various houses in the eastern United States, as well as friends in New Jersey.

Shortly after the Jubilee, the priests of their religious province held a convention, or chapter. The purpose of this meeting was to elect new superiors and address other provincial business. These conventions are typically held every three years, and members are expected to be prepared for any reassignments that may result. The passage ends by stating that the author considered a subsequent development involving Father M. to be fortunate.

Anyhow, they sent me thither to help him celebrate and, Thank God, we had a very pleasant celebration of about a week or ten days. Thanks be to God. It was about 12 years since my 20 year sojourn in the Empire State, and Fr. M. J. had, in about 7 years, made quite some friends in the same three stations where I had been located ahead of him. A number of our cousins from Boston and elsewhere, including two nuns, attended the solemn Mass as the climax of the celebration, which, Thank God, "went off without a hitch." The following days we visited our different houses in the East, and besides some friends in N. J. Shortly after that celebration the Fathers of our Province held a chapter or convention, for election of new superiors and other affairs of the Province. Such chapters, as a rule, are held every 3 years, and everyone is supposed to be ready for a change, if such come. Fortunately, it seemed to me, and providen- tially, Fr. M.

In response, a woman referred to as the mother sighed. The narrator suggests this was because she was recalling the difficulties of that era, which she felt overshadowed the pleasant memories. She then quietly said, "Thanks be to God, I'm glad it's over!"

The narrator has frequently reflected on this incident and considers the mother's exclamation to be a beautiful and truly Christian sentiment.
styled: Probably you remember when, at the Golden Wedding in 1913 we were all musing over scenes and events on the River Bank and in old Trimbelle someone remarked: "Wouldn't it be nice if we could go back there again!", dear Mother, gently sighing as if revisioning the trials of those days, outweighing the beauties and pleasures -- half whispered an exclamation: "Thanks be to God, I'm glad it's over !" The writer copes with nostalgia by remembering that their childhood home was already undergoing sad changes before they left. These memories include scenes of "burned hills," the "Big Ravine," prairie fires, and a place called the "little Poplars."

The poplars were beautiful during the day in spring but felt lonely in the evening. The writer recounts an incident that happened there to the person being addressed, Jimmy Casey. One evening, when it was almost dark, Jimmy was on his way home and encountered an animal he later concluded must have been a lynx.

Before he became scared, Jimmy mistook the animal for the writer (whose name is apparently Barney) and called out, "Is that you Barney?" This question served as an unintentional bluff. The lynx did not respond but instead jumped into a thicket, allowing Jimmy to pass. The writer notes that the animal's silent retreat was the best possible outcome.

After the encounter, Jimmy ran home extremely fast over a hill and through several hollows. He was about 13 years old at the time.

Of course, neither of us answered, except, on its part, which was perhaps the best answer we could give under the circum- stances, when it leaped into the ticket and let Jimmy Casey pass. It is not hard to reckon the amount of grass that grew, or that didn't grow, under his feet till Jimmy was over the hill and home over big and little hollows. You must have been about 13 at the time.

The passage begins by presenting two poetic expressions of a similar theme. The first suggests that high ideals and aspirations are inevitably destroyed by the harshness of reality. The second, attributed to a poet named Moor, reinforces this by describing life as a difficult journey where human faculties like imagination and reason only illuminate the troubles; according to this view, true peace can only be found in a spiritual afterlife.

Following these reflections, the narrator recounts a travel plan that began on August 11th. The intention was to depart from St. Bonaventure's Monastery in Detroit and take a train to Chicago, then continue to Marathon, Wisconsin, on the same day. In Marathon, the narrator was scheduled to meet a Father Maurice and then travel with him to St. Paul the following day to meet a Father Edward.

Although the narrator arrived at the station on time, they missed the train. At the time, this was perceived as a personal failure resulting from a foolish mistake. Later, however, the event was reinterpreted as being fortunate and the result of a divine plan. This change in perspective occurred three weeks later, after the narrator had visited Marathon. They then realized that missing the initial train had prevented an unnecessary round trip of 130 miles (65 miles each way) at the beginning of the journey.
styled: And I said: In the world each ideal that sines like a star on life's wave is wrecked on the shores of the real and sleeps like a dream in a grave." Quite in the same spirit too, Moor beautifully tunes in: "Poor wanderers of a stormy day, from wave to wave we're driven; And fancy's flash and reason's ray serve but to light the troubled way ; -- There's nothing calm but Heaven. " Well to get started at last: I left St. Bonaventure's Monastery, Detroit, August 11th, planning to catch the first train to Chi- cago, thence to Marathon, Wis. same day, where I'd meet Fr. Maurice and go with him next day to St. Paul where Fr. Edward was expecting us. I was in time for the train o.k. but for- tunately failed to catch it. The Dear Lord had planned other- wise: though at the time it did seem to me as the result of nothing less than stupidity on my part. It was only three weeks later, having been to Marathon for the first time, I realized that missing the train that morning saved me twice 65 miles on starting out.

The experiences of earthly life, including both its pleasures and its trials, are presented as brief and insignificant when compared to the rewards of an eternal afterlife.

According to this view, the value of worldly experiences is limited to two functions:
1.  To sustain a person through life until death.
2.  To reduce excessive attachment to the material world and to self-interest, which are described as common deceptions.

To support this point, the passage cites Fr. Ryan's book "Son of the Mystic," stating that it is futile to expect to find true inner peace except through serving and trusting in God. The specific quote provided, "I walked in the world with the worldly, I craved what the world never gave," is used to illustrate that a life focused on worldly pursuits leads to unfulfillment because the world cannot provide what a person truly desires.

A change in travel plans resulted in a journey that was approximately 300 miles shorter. The author perceived this change and the resulting positive social connections as being divinely prearranged and otherwise impossible.

Instead of traveling to Marathon, the author went to Milwaukee with a stop in Chicago. At the station in Chicago, an old friend, John Gorman, met the author with his family and insisted they have dinner at a hotel. Although the author had not felt hungry or even thought about food, they realized they were after having consumed only a cup of coffee and a small piece of bread in the preceding 12 hours. The author attributed the friend's charitable offer of a meal to God's awareness of their needs.

That night, the author had an enjoyable evening at the S. Francis monastery. This location was significant as it was the first monastery the author had visited 40 years prior, while on their way to the Novitiate. The next morning, after attending Mass, the author made a long-distance phone call to an individual identified as "Fr."
styled: Altogether it saved me about 300 miles and, as if all prearranged, enabled me to make happy and unexpected con- nections which I would hardly have found possible to make other - wise. Thanks be to God! Instead of to Marathon, I went to Milwaukee, after a very pleasant little repast in Chicago with an old friend, John Gorman and family, who met me at the depot and insisted on us going to a nearby hotel and having dinner. I had not felt particularly hungry at all -- in fact I'd not thought of eating -- but found that close to 12 hours on a cup of coffee and a small slice of bread had provided quite a vacancy when we sat down to a well spread table. This travel plan allowed the writer to depart from Milwaukee at 2:00 PM, providing sufficient time to visit the various houses of their organization and meet with members of their religious community. The alternative would have been to leave on the Omaha train at 10:00 AM.

In addition to this priest and the group of nuns, there were several other members of religious orders on board.

Until the train began to depart from New Lisbon, the writer had been uncertain how these other religious passengers perceived them, wondering if they were being mistaken for a venerable rabbi or another type of respected or idealized figure.

Two individuals, a deacon and a sub-deacon, assisted Father Edward at a formal Jubilee Mass after having already conducted their own Masses earlier. Bishop Reverman was in official attendance, and Father Weber delivered the sermon. Father Weber now holds the position of Vicar General and appears to be in good health.

The Mass and its associated receptions were successful.

A narrator, a priest who had worn a beard for over 40 years, was traveling on a crowded coach, and he believed his appearance made him somewhat conspicuous.

He was accompanied by another priest, identified as Father M. Joachim. Upon entering the vehicle, each carrying a bag, Father M. Joachim drew attention to them by stopping and exclaiming in a loud voice, "Glory be to God! Look at all the sisters." The narrator noted that the other passengers seemed to expect such a comment from one of the older, bearded men.

Later, while the coach was crossing the Mississippi River at La Crosse, a third priest, described as friendly-looking, was pointing out the sights downstream. The narrator quietly advised this priest, "Father; Look upstream."

At this suggestion, the friendly-looking priest lost all interest in the scenery. He approached the front seat where the narrator and his companion were sitting and offered his hand to the narrator, asking if he was Father Maurice Casey.

The narrator corrected the man's mistake. While Father M. Joachim raised his hand in greeting, the narrator clarified, "This is Father Maurice."

The reunion of these two priests—Father M. Joachim (who was, in fact, Father Maurice) and the other priest—became the focus of attention for the other passengers. The two men had been students together 30 years before and had not met since they were ordained.
styled: The coach was well filled, and the beard I carried -- had carried more than 40 years -- made me no doubt, at least a little conspicuous. Well, if there had been any misgivings in that direction, Fr. M. Joachim positively settled it with one happy exclamation. As we entered through the vestibule, each with a grip, he stopped as in astonishment and in a clear voice that everyone seemed expecting from one of the gray-beards, called out: "Glory be to God! Look at all the sisters." Crossing the Mississippi (at LaCrosse) , shortly after, said friendly looking priest was calling attention to beauties down the River when I called to him in a half whisper: "Father ; Look upstream. " With that, he seemed to forget the scenery altogether and, coming up to our front seat offered me his hand, asking: "Are you not Fr. Maurice Casey?" "Why!" I answered, as Fr. M. J.'s hand raised to meet his, "This is Father Maurice." All attention seemed on the two of them. They had studied together 30 years before and had not met since ordination.

The travelers journeyed quickly along the Minnesota side of the river, passing through several towns. One of these was Redwing, which is where a man named Father Solanus first saw railroad cars in the year 1880. Another was Hastings, where an individual referred to as "Mother" had worked during her youth.

As the sun set over the hills, their journey continued alongside a scenic, wide section of the river, concluding with their arrival at the Union Depot in St. Paul.

At the station, they met a man named Father Edward. This was their first meeting with him since he had returned from the Philippines.

They also telephoned a man named Mike Costello. This individual has several past connections to the people involved:
*   Sixty years prior, he was the boyfriend of the person to whom the original message was addressed.
*   Fifty years prior, he shared living quarters with the writer of the message. At that time, they were working at the Stillwater Penitentiary, where the writer was an unskilled laborer and Costello was a boiler-maker.
*   The writer notes that their dormitory was situated outside the prison walls, implying they had some form of special influence or privilege.

Currently, Mike Costello holds the rank of sergeant on the St. Paul Police Force.

A person named Mildred, who is known to the recipient of the original message, had arranged a small and pleasant reception for the travelers. She organized this event with her friends, the Conley family, and they hosted it together.
styled: Before we knew it, we were speeding up the Minnesota side on through Redwing, where in 1880 Father Solanus saw railroad cars the first time, and Hastings, where Mother worked as a girl, till across and around the beautiful widening in the River, we watched the great red sun dip to the hills while we glided toward St. Paul and into the Union Depot. Here we met Fr. Edward -- first time since his return from the Philippines. We phoned to your boy-friend of 60 years ago, Mike Costello, and my bed-fellow 10 years later when I was a "roust-a-bout" and he a boiler-maker in the Stillwater Penitentiary. Our dormitory, however, was outside the walls, so we had a "pull" of some kind. Mike is now a sergeant on the St. Paul Police Force. Your Mildred had arranged with her friends, the Conley family, to give us (as indeed they did together with herself) an ideally pleasant little reception.

This account, likely from the month of August, describes a visit to Joseph's Convent near the city's East end. The writer notes a significant change over 50 years, as the convent's community has grown from just two or three members to an estimated thirty. The writer told the current residents about personally transporting the original members to and from school on trolley cars, a memory that one of the long-time residents also recalled. During the visit, the writer administered Holy Communion to a resident who was gravely ill.

Later that afternoon, the writer and companions went to a neighborhood known as the "Steel Plant" to perform a blessing for a ten-year-old girl, who was the granddaughter of a teacher named Aggie Murphy Oteir, as well as for others. The writer was surprised that Aggie Murphy Oteir's appearance had changed very little in the 26 years since they had last seen her at Father M. Joachim's first Mass.

From there, the group crossed the St. Louis River into Duluth, where they met with old friends from Hudson.

The next day, a Tuesday, was busy due to a planned trip. At approximately 2:00 PM, they departed for St. Paul on a modern train. The route went through St. Cloud and Minneapolis, and they arrived in St. Paul between 5:30 PM and 6:00 PM.
styled: Joseph's Convent, down near the East end. What a change in 50 years! They wondered when I told them that I used to carry them on the trolley-cars as they went daily back and forth to school -- only two or three in the whole community. Now they must number about thirty in that Convent, as seemed to me. One of them present remembered those pioneer days. To another, now an invalid seemingly just waiting to take off for Heaven I had the privilege of giving Holy Communion. Deo Gratias. That P. M. we went to bless a little ten year old grand- daughter of Teacher Aggie Murphy Oteir in the "Steel Plant", and some others. I was surprised at the seemingly little change in her appearance in twenty-six years, when she attended Fr. M. Joachim's first Holy Mass. Thence we crossed over St. Louis River to Duluth where we found some old friends from Hudson. Tuesday was short and busy, from the fact that we were to leave for St. Paul about 2 P.m. We arrived via St. Cloud and Minneapolis about 5:30-6 P.m. It was an up-to-date train. Aug.

After a meal, a woman arranged a surprise long-distance phone call from Seattle. The call allowed a group to speak with individuals named Pat, Emma, Guss, and the person being addressed. For one of the participants, it was the first conversation with these individuals in 25 years, since a Golden Wedding anniversary.

The group found suitable lodging at the College of St. Thomas. A person named Father Edward had previously been the Rector of this college but resigned before traveling to Australia and the Philippines. The next day, after a religious service and breakfast at a convent, where a Father M.J. and another individual assisted each other, the group made some visits. Around 2:00 PM, they left for the city of Superior, routing through Sault Ste. Marie and arriving between 5:30 and 6:00 PM.

At the station in Superior, the group was met by their friends, Ed Sampson and his wife. The Sampsons drove them to the Parish House located at 12th and John Streets. The meeting was anticipated, as Mrs. Sampson had previously telephoned a member of the group before they left Detroit. In that call, she mentioned that she and her husband were beginning their vacation and that they might meet in Superior.

The next day, which was the Feast of the Assumption, a pleasant celebration was held. A person identified as Father M. was also present or involved.

We found ideal quarters in the College of St. Thomas, where Fr. Edward had been Rector before his resignation prior to going to Australia and the Philippines. We made some calls next day after Holy Mass and Breakfast -- Fr. M. J. and I serving each other in turn at the Convent -- and about 2 P.M. left via Sault Ste. Marie to reach Superior about 5:30 -6 o'clock. The celebration next day, Feast of the Assumption, was a happy one. Fr. M.

The narrator describes recently performing a Mass at the same location where they first attended a solemn Midnight Mass celebrated by three priests.

This first experience took place on Christmas Eve in 1881. On that occasion, a large group of people, including the narrator, traveled ten miles in new sleighs pulled by the Ryans' horses. The temperature was extremely cold, starting at -18°F and dropping to -22°F by the time they returned home. The narrator recalls the ceremonies as being beautifully inspiring and felt a sense of gratitude.

At this location, there is now a school. The narrator remembers that in 1886 or 1887, a group of men broke ground for the school for a priest named Father Kelly. This group consisted of the narrator's father, Maurice, Mr. Ryan, Matt and Peter Welsh, and a young Jim Pachingham. Father Kelly was overjoyed by this and insisted that the group have a celebratory dinner at a place called Reilly's. He was so moved with appreciation that he had tears in his eyes, which the narrator felt was more expressive than any words.

Later that morning, the narrator's group went for a hike, climbing a bluff to the south of the city. From the top, there was a view described as surprisingly beautiful, which included the city, the St. Croix River, the nearby city of Stillwater, and the layout of the new State Prison. In the distance to the right, Mount St. Helen was also visible.
styled: I had the privilege once more of offering the Holy Sacrifice where for the first time I had attended a solemn Mass -- three priests -- and that at Midnight. It was Christmas Eve in 1881 when with Ryans' roadsters and our new sleighs a real load of us started in the ten miles when it was 18 below zero, and before we got home it was 22 below. The ceremonies were beautifully inspiring. Thanks be to God! They have a fine school now where in 1886 or 1887 Papa and Maurice and Mr. Ryan, Matt and Peter Welsh and young Jim Pachingham broke ground for dear Fr. Kelly. How happy he was, insisting that we come down to Reilly's and have a good dinner. Tears of appreciation filled his eyes, more expressive than any words he could have uttered. Later in the morning we went for a hike, climbing the bluff to the south whence is a surprisingly beautiful view, not only of the city itself and the St. Croix River, but of Stillwater and the new State Prison layout, with Mt. St. Helen in the distance to the right.

The author expresses a deep nostalgic affection for St. Michael's. They speculate that while the surrounding views are likely as beautiful to the current younger generation as they were 50 or 60 years prior, the author's own experience of these scenes is imbued with a unique and powerful personal significance. Of all the locations, the author felt the strongest desire to spend more time inside the church itself, as it seemed to have remained unchanged over the years.

The group then drove quickly down Third Avenue and the steep Chestnut Street. The author notes that Chestnut Street is where they learned to operate trolley cars in 1887. styled: The old mill at Burkhardt would seem to have been shell shocked or something like that. According to the most recent information available, Anna and Emma were living together again on the farm.

The group's next stop was the Diehl-Germain residence. The occupants, an elderly couple named Anna and Joe, were surprised by the visit.

styled: Edward and I climbed the old entrance to the Roberts Estate. We found, I'm inclined to say, poor little Emma, so modest and winsome in school-days and later when Fr. The older of the two, Anna, perhaps more ambitious, married and became a venerated grandma. One of her four sons, I believe, became a professor at Cornell. The mother belonged some way to the O'Brien family and, consequently, seemed to hope that we might stay for the funeral and possibly conduct it, and offer the Mass. Returning from the Bowers, between 2 and 3 P.M., what seemed to the writer a happy feature of the day's program, was proposed. We were to go to "The Bluff".

A group of travelers, including individuals identified as Father Maurice, Father Edward, and Father S., decided to go to a place called Trimbelle. They chose to take an old wagon road for their journey. This route was preferable to two alternatives: traveling half a mile north of the Elsworth Highway or taking a road that followed the Mississippi River.

Initially, the group began to regret their choice for the 13-mile, down-river portion of their trip. However, their minds changed when they turned onto a well-traveled road to their right and a neat, white house became visible through the trees. The narrator notes that in 1878, these trees had only been small bushes. Upon seeing the house, Father Maurice identified it as "Aunt Mary's old house," and his neighbor confirmed this.

At the house, Father Edward got out of their vehicle to ask for directions to the River Road that led to Diamond Bluff. Father S. also approached the house, hoping to at least look inside, as it was a place where he had spent a happy time 59 years earlier.

The passage includes an anecdote from that visit 59 years prior. During his two-week stay, Father S. attended a court case in Prescott. While the court was in session, he sat in Judge Ross's chair, not understanding at the time why this action amused the people in the courtroom.

Fortunately, we took the old wagon road, rather than going a half mile north ot the Elsworth Highway, or down to that, following the course of the "Father of Waters". We were begin- ning to think we had made a mistake in not taking the latter for the 13 mile down-the-river trip, when, turning on a fairly trod road to the right, a neat little white house loomed through the trees (small bushes at my visit in 1878) and Fr. The author, Paul, was in the "Twin Cities" (Minneapolis-St. Paul) and was determined to perform a Catholic Mass. This decision created a conflict with his travel schedule, as the only other train to Chicago that day, aside from his own, was leaving in 30 minutes. He also wanted to arrive in Detroit by the following morning, a Saturday.

The journey had been marked by bad weather. It had been raining since the group left Seattle on Tuesday evening and had snowed while they crossed the Rocky Mountains. In the Twin Cities, storm clouds were gathering around the skyscrapers. The situation was further complicated because the St. Paul Union Station had burned down two days prior, and the area remained disorganized.

At the station, the author had a brief but warm encounter with a Sergeant Costello, who was an acquaintance of the person the author was addressing. The meeting was short because Costello was busy, and the author was in a hurry. Costello was prepared for the storm, but the author was not, and it had begun to rain lightly.

Faced with these circumstances, the author briefly hesitated. With no time for deliberation and having no umbrella, he initially decided against performing the Mass and started to head back to his train, which was preparing to depart.

Despite this, the author ultimately did perform the Mass. To accommodate this, two trains were held. The author expressed gratitude for this outcome, which he considered an act of God.

The Union Depot in St. Paul had been burned to the ground the day before yesterday, and, as yet, order and con- fusion were still wrangling for mastery. Your above referred to barefoot boy-friend -- now Sergeant Costello -- was on the scene, and gave me a warm greeting, mutually brief, however, for he was busy and I was in a hurry. He was prepared for the threatened storm and, as yet, I was able to dodge the drops or ignore them. HOLY MASS OFFERED -- TWO TRAINS HELD -- THANKS BE TO GOD Under such circumstances, I surely did hesitate: briefly, however, for there was really no time for deliberation. Having no umbrella, I started back to our train about to start off.

Immediately after a light breakfast, the writer took a trolley to the train station, which was about half a mile away.

At the station, the writer asked a person who appeared to be an official if there was a train to Chicago. The official confirmed that the train just arriving was headed there. The train, named the "Burlington," stopped almost immediately. The writer boarded, and it departed at full speed. It was running three hours behind schedule, with its first stop set for Point Douglas.

This part of the journey was personally significant for the writer. The train's route passed several memorable locations:
*   The place where the writer first appreciated the beauty of the natural landscape.
*   A spot along the Mississippi River, about four miles downstream, where the writer had played on the sand as a child.
*   The confluence of the St. Croix and Mississippi rivers.
*   The town of Prescott, where the writer and four other people had been baptized.

Reflecting on the experience, the writer felt they were not as grateful as they should have been for these memories at that moment, but hoped to become more appreciative in the future.
styled: After breakfast, needless to say, no heavy one -- I lost no time in catching a trolley and getting over the half-mile or so to the station. "Is there any train for Chicago today?" I asked what seemed to be an official just waving a train backing in to stop. "Yes" he answered courteously "Here is one now". He hardly finished speaking, when, stopped was the train; on I stepped: and off went the "Burlington" at full speed; three hours late, its first stop at Point Douglas. I need not tell you what that meant to me. It took me past where I first saw the beauties of God's visible creation, down the Mississippi, where I played in the sand of its beautiful shore some four miles below; having crossed the mouth of the beautiful St. Croix and shot past Prescott where five of us had received Baptism. I certainly was not a tenth as grateful as I ought to have been, but I hope to be more so some day.

The narrator does not specifically recall being anxious about making the train connection in Chicago but presumes they likely were to some extent. During the storm, just before reaching LaCrosse, the train passed a burning farmhouse that the narrator thought had been struck by lightning.

The train arrived in Chicago five hours late, at nearly 10:30 PM. The narrator asked a baggage master about a connecting train to Detroit and was informed that the last one had been scheduled to depart around 6:00 PM. Additionally, that train left from a different station, which was a 20-minute trolley ride away from the Burlington station where the narrator had arrived.
styled: I had reckoned, at all events, that it would please the Divine Lover of our poor souls and be good for mine especially to offer that Holy Mass; and that it would be a very easy thing for the Great God and Governor of the Universe to hold any train He might wish me to take. Besides, that train was supposed to leave from a station about a twenty minute trolley ride from that of the "Burlington".

Despite this advice and the time pressure, the narrator proceeded to conduct the Mass and also spent a short time in prayer afterward.

The narrator recounts a journey where a group of people, including individuals named Father Maurice and Father Barney, were traveling. The narrator makes a brief digression to recall a previous conclusion that a certain location was about two miles below a place called "the Bluff."

This group had a custom of praying the Rosary at the beginning of their longer trips. On this particular day, however, they had already traveled for about twenty miles through hills and valleys and were moving quickly toward a mountain when they realized they had forgotten. Father Maurice pointed this out and prompted Father Barney to lead the prayer, which he then started.

The author anticipates that one might question how it is possible to pray effectively without distraction under such circumstances. The author states they have no special technique for this. Instead, they reframe the issue, proposing that the important question is not how to avoid distractions, but whether distractions during prayer are displeasing to God.

The author's personal belief is that such distractions do not displease God. This is consistent with advice the author gives to people who are overly anxious or meticulous about their religious observances: that God is not unreasonable or difficult to please, and therefore, imperfect or distracted prayer is acceptable.

During a journey, a group of at least four people was traveling around a mountain. One of them, Father Edward, was seeing the Trimbelle landscape for the first time. The narrator views this landscape as a timeless expression of divine creation. Deeply impressed, Father Edward simply exclaimed, "This is beautiful!"

Soon after, the group arrived in the village of Alihue. The narrator recognized it from a visit sixty years prior. While the village was still neat and tidy, it and its surroundings seemed smaller to the narrator than they remembered.

The narrator recalls that Alihue's population used to be predominantly Protestant, with denominations including Methodists and Lutherans, and that the village frequently held religious revivals. At that time, the narrator and their companions were likely the nearest Catholics to the village. The narrator describes the villagers of that period as honest and good people according to their own Christian beliefs.

In the present day, approximately a dozen children were playing on the village green near a modest, separate building. This led the narrator to speculate they might be waiting for Sunday school. The children stopped playing to look at the visitors. The narrator presumes the children's curiosity was due to the sight of two older, bearded men wearing unfamiliar attire.

At that moment, the narrator was occupied leading a Rosary prayer. The narrator states that if they had not been engaged in this prayer, they would have offered the children a blessing.

The writing takes place on the evening of July 14th, a day the writer identifies as the feast day of St. Bonaventure, and continues on July 15th.

He interprets the illness, which lasted about ten days, as the most severe penance he, as "the sinner Solanus," has ever undergone. He is writing the conclusion to his description of Father Edward's Jubilee and a trip to "The Bluff" and Trimbelle that occurred at that time. He gives two reasons for continuing now: first, he has received a hopeful letter from a "Father M. Joachim" indicating a significant change in attitude and a desire to return to the monastery. The recipient's specific reason for gratitude is their survival through several narrow escapes from danger during the previous ten months. The writer suggests that these threatening experiences should be viewed as significant struggles. The writer also had a similar difficult experience, beginning around September 10th of the previous year, which involved a severe case of influenza along with a varicose condition in the ankle.

At a Mass attended by Bishop Griffin, Father Solanus gave a sermon he had been appointed to deliver several months prior. This was his first time preaching in the presence of a bishop. According to the narrator, Father Solanus was personally dissatisfied with his sermon, feeling it was not as good as it should have been. The narrator does not clearly recall how others received it.

A significant disappointment for Father Solanus occurred during the service when no one except the priest celebrating the Mass received Holy Communion. The narrator reflects that it was perhaps fortunate Father Solanus had not anticipated this. Apart from that issue, the event proceeded smoothly.

After the service, a large crowd was waiting outside the church. It included numerous members of the Mangan family, among whom the narrator recognized a person named Tim and a few others. Also present was the oldest person there, Bill Betzel, who was 93 years old at the time. The narrator notes that Betzel would be 98 at the time of writing, if still living.

Mr. Betzel's 87-year-old wife, who was blind and an invalid, had requested to see Father Solanus and the narrator. After dinner, they visited her, and she wept when they gave her a blessing.
styled: Bishop Griffin present. Fr. Solanus had been appointed several months before or about the same as appointed to give the sermon. It was his first time before a Bishop and I hardly remember if it was satisfactory. For himself it was far from what it ought to have been. Perhaps it was fortunate that he did not forsee what caused him quite a dissapointment before the Mass was over - No one except the Rev. Celebrant received Holy Communion: .... Otherwise everything went off without a hitch. Deo Gratias. But what a crowd waiting outside after the celebration in Church! One Mangan after an- other each with a family. Tim. and one or two of the others I recog- nized. And among the many others the senior of them all, now the 98 year-old Bill Betzel, if he still lives. He was 93 then, and his wife who was blind and an invalid 87 years-old wished to see us. So after dinner we visited her and she wept when we gave her cur blessing.

The narrator, Joseph, was at a location known as St. Joseph's, which overlooked the Mississippi River from a height of approximately 400 feet, and he was experiencing a powerful emotional response to the view.

The previous night, the narrator and a priest, Father Maurice J., had traveled to a place called St. Mary's Big River. They were driven from St. Paul, by way of River Falls and Hudson, by a man named Dean Conley. The narrator notes that at the time of this trip, they only suspected what they now know to be true: that Conley would eventually become the narrator's nephew-in-law. Conley is also identified as the third son of an individual called "Br. Jim." The narrator reflects that had they known this for certain during the drive, it would have enhanced their enjoyment of the journey.

At St. Mary's, the narrator and Father Maurice J. conducted Mass. This church held personal significance for them, as it was the place where the older members of their group had first attended Mass and received religious instruction (Catechism), and was also where Maurice had his First Communion ceremony. They conducted the first scheduled Mass of the day because the church's resident pastor was away attending to a mission located several miles from the church. The narrator felt some envy for the pastor who was traveling to the mission but acknowledged that this duty rightfully belonged to the pastor. The narrator also mentions enjoying the short sermon that was delivered during their service.

After they finished their post-service prayers, the pastor, who had by then returned from his mission, drove them quickly along the Prescott-Elsworth Highway. They soon arrived at the sacristy of St. Joseph's, where they began to put on their vestments in preparation for a formal religious service that would involve a high-ranking cleric, a Right Reverend.

Maurice J. and I had gone out to St. Mary's Big River the night before; Dean Conley having driven us down from St. Paul via River Falls, and Hudson. (Hardly necessary now to say who same D.C. was. It might've added somewhat to the already exquisit pleasure of the trip had we recognized in him what we only surmised at the time, a future nephew-in-law and ... Br. Jim's third son). We had offered our holy Masses out at said old St. Mary's where we older ones first went to holy Mass and to Catechism instructions, down to Maurice receiving First Holy Communion. We took the first scheduled Mass while the Rev. Pastor went to his mission several miles distant. I was inclined to envy him the privilege but felt that it was coming to him rather than to his younger brother but I quite enjoyed his nice little sermon. After our thanksgiving, etc, the pastor having returned reshot us down the Prescott-Elsworth Highway and before we knew it we were in the St. Joseph's sacristy vesting for solemn services, Rt. Rev.

The author of this letter is writing to their niece, Dorothy, on the Feast of Saint Joseph, the spouse of Mary. They express a hope that Saint Joseph is watching over Dorothy and her family.

The author has been intending to write for several months and has been thinking about Dorothy since a memorable day they spent together with her family on a mountain overlooking Mount Rainier. They note with surprise that nearly three years have passed since that meeting.

This reflection leads the author to contemplate mortality. They wonder how much time they and Dorothy have left before they die, joining the many loved ones who have already passed away. They specifically mention a "Brother Guss" as a notable person who has died since their meeting at the mountain.

The author then decides not to spend more time on memories, stating that past events are fleeting and insubstantial, like soap bubbles. They believe that focusing on the past is a waste of time unless it relates to what they consider life's single most important purpose. This purpose is to better understand, love, and serve God in order to ensure the salvation of one's soul.
styled: My Dear Niece Dorothy: - God bless you this dear, beautiful Feast of the most priviliged Spouse of Mary. May be too be watching over you and yours! I've been wanting to write you these many months. Indeed you have been on my mind quite a little ever since that memorable day we conclude with you and your little family on the "mount" in view of the majestic "old Ranier. Who would believe that nearly three years has passed since that day? How many more-times three, till we follow so many of our dear ones gone ahead of that land-mark event, and join even those who have followed since? -- poor, dear Brother Guss, (at least for me), one of the notables. I would like to continue playing with memories but time forbids me to waste it on events that have passed and do pass like soap-bubles, no matter how grand and gaudy, unless they pertain to the one thing necessary - knowing God better so as to love Him and serve Him better and save our immortal souls.

A formal Mass was planned to commemorate the 36th anniversary of an individual named M's ordination. However, due to the small and temporary nature of the chapel, the plan was altered. Instead, the writer and M assisted one another in their separate services, and the writer was impressed with M's capability. The service took place on a Wednesday, which marked the anniversary of M's first Mass, rather than on the Monday anniversary of the ordination itself.

The writer had committed to an individual known as the Father Guardian, who was unwell at the time, to try to return by Sunday. Fulfilling this required an important visit to a sick person in Royal Oak (near Detroit), a detour that added 375 miles or more to the journey.

A man who is a Jewish convert drove the writer from Detroit. This driver is described as very intelligent, and there is a hope that he will become a priest. The writer, the driver, and others had an enjoyable visit on Saturday evening and Sunday. A Father John, who was part of the group, had to leave with the others around 5:00 PM on Sunday to return for his classes on Monday morning.

The writer is sending the recipient two letters that are expected to be interesting, along with a photograph taken over a year ago. The writer makes the logical observation that the subject of the photo looks younger in the picture than they do in person now.

The central point of the passage is the supreme importance of compromise for achieving peace within a family. It advises that for a family to be harmonious, each spouse should adjust their personal preferences and ideals to align with those of their partner. Furthermore, it is presented as a way to convince people that the possibility of achieving one's ultimate spiritual goals is infinitely more valuable than the relatively minor personal sacrifices required in a marriage.

To illustrate this, an example is given from around the year 1904. At that time, both the Catholic and the general press were giving extensive attention to Leo Tolstoy, who was widely regarded as a prominent genius of the age.

The main points are:

*   **Guidance through Prayer:** It advises seeking divine guidance, specifically by praying to St. Joseph and the "Poor Souls" (a Catholic term for souls in Purgatory).

*   **A Proposed Spiritual Partnership:** A specific strategy is suggested for engaging the Poor Souls, especially one's deceased relatives. The idea is to invite them to participate in and assist with missionary work. In exchange for their spiritual assistance, one would promise them a share, such as a percentage of the "profits" or benefits that result from the work.

*   **The Concept of "Double Charity":** This act is described as a "double charity" because it serves two groups simultaneously:
    1.  It benefits living people on Earth (referred to as the "Church militant"), by supporting missionaries and their efforts.
    2.  It benefits the deceased souls undergoing purification (the "Church suffering").

*   **Supporting Evidence from an Anecdote:** To support the principle that charitable giving leads to success, the text cites the example of John D. Rockefeller. It claims that Rockefeller's great financial success was widely attributed to his practice of consistently donating about 10% of his profits to charitable works. The author of the passage states that this report is credible and that they have seen similar principles lead to positive results in other cases.

*   **Concluding Remarks:** The passage ends with a note that the author's attempt to conclude briefly was unsuccessful, illustrating the proverb, "The more hurry, the less speed." It closes with a plea for divine help.

While there, he met and shared living quarters with a man named Mike, who was a boilermaker, and Mike's partner, who was a general laborer. Their sleeping area was located outside the main prison wall.

In the years that followed, one of these men became a lieutenant in the St. Paul police department, and the other became a Capuchin friar and a priest.

The author provides this background to explain a more recent situation. After not seeing Mike in person for over thirty years (though they had spoken on the phone), the author visited him. At the time of the visit, Mike was in his 80s, nearly blind, and appeared to be energized by the visit.

This long history is relevant because, several weeks prior, individuals referred to as "the O'Donnell Friends" had been disappointed about an issue. The author felt certain that this disappointment was the result of a mistake or a hidden misunderstanding. This belief was confirmed to be correct, which the author considers a positive outcome for all involved and a fortunate development that may have initially seemed negative.

The author concludes by advising the recipient that as they get to know these same friends, whom the author has known for several years, the nature of their relationship will likely change. The author predicts that the recipient will eventually come to feel that they are working collaboratively *with* these friends, rather than simply working *for* them.

This communication is intended to offer support and perspective to friends who are traveling and have expressed concern about falling prices. The author provides three points to help ease their anxiety.

First, the author suggests that financial success and material possessions are not of primary importance. Because these things are temporary and will inevitably be lost, one should not sacrifice their inner peace by worrying about them.

Second, the author proposes that making financial mistakes can be a positive force for character development. Such setbacks can be viewed as opportunities to cultivate humility.

Finally, the author offers a practical, economic reason for the current situation. It is a presidential election year, which typically causes a temporary downturn in prices, particularly for farm goods. This happens because businesses tend to delay investments until the election is over, creating market uncertainty. This suggests the price drop is a predictable, short-term trend rather than a lasting problem.
styled: Febr.22nd. My Dear Friends: God bless you one and all. Just a word to meet you down there as friend from up north. I hope it may please the Lord to bring you back in better weather and brighter hopes than saw you start on the trip I'd like to have made with you. Permit me to follow in spirit! At the same time, seeing your rather undue concern at dropping prices, etc, I thought a word of observation might help a little to steady someone's nerves. First of all, however, we should re-remember at all events, that success or want of the same is not essential as pertains temporalities. Sooner or later we shall have to drop them - if they don't drop us first. Why, therefore, lose our peace on their account? Then again, God often permits us to make temporal blunders in order to foster humility in our souls so that in the sight of Heaven we may be more amible. Finally this is "Presidential Election year." That means more or less a depression in farm prices at least till after Election-day. Business men will not invest till Election.

The author also acknowledges a recent correspondence or item from the recipient, Joseph, which was received last week. The author apologizes for not mentioning this during a phone call two nights prior. Well-wishes are extended to Joseph and his family, with a specific mention of his wife.

The background on Father Guardian's health is as follows:

About a year ago, Father Guardian, whose first name was Matthias, became seriously ill. For several months, up until early March, his condition prevented him from attending meals in the dining hall or participating in choir services. During this period, he slept very little and was only able to do so while sitting in a chair.

Apparently, during his illness, Father Guardian read a biography of the late Bishop Hartman of India, who is described as a significant modern missionary. Afterward, he performed a novena, a nine-day period of prayer, in Bishop Hartman's honor. The purpose of this prayer was to petition for an intervention that would allow him to recover enough to fulfill the principal duties of his position.

This is necessary due to a heavy workload of correspondence, which includes writing to approximately twenty other people in addition to Mrs. O'Donnell's relation, J.J. This message is from Father Solanus, a Capuchin friar, to a Mrs. O'Donnell.

He begins by identifying her location, which he describes as being in what was once considered a rugged pioneer area of the American West. He provides specific geographic details, noting that her location is across the Mississippi River, about 25 miles upriver from his own birthplace, which itself was 4 miles below Prescott. He states that in the year 1870, this region was indeed a frontier but was also a very scenic part of the country.

The author reports that he and another person named Joe have discussed Mrs. O'Donnell's situation and are very pleased to learn that her unspecified problem or illness has been successfully controlled and that the outlook is now promising. He expresses his personal hope that the most difficult part of her ordeal is now over and was connected to the end of the previous year.

He then presents a religious perspective on hardship, referencing the belief that God sends trials to those He loves. Based on this concept, he advises that suffering can be seen as a privilege to be thankful for, as it is a way for a person to become more like God.

The message concludes with the author wishing Mrs. O'Donnell and her family well and hoping for her speedy recovery.

From this viewpoint, both the joys and the sorrows experienced within life are, in themselves, trivial and insignificant. People who focus on worldly matters are seen as mistakenly treating this temporary existence as the ultimate reality.

Despite being considered fundamentally unimportant, these emotions are nevertheless viewed as necessary and helpful due to human weaknesses. They serve two distinct, practical functions:

A solemn high Mass was held on the day of writing to mark the 35th anniversary of the first Mass celebrated by the writer's brother, Maurice Joachim. This original ceremony took place in Superior, Wisconsin, in 1911. Maurice Joachim is now in St. Paul, Minnesota, with Right Reverend Brother Edward, who has returned from the Philippines.

Brother Edward was rescued from an internment camp in the Philippines on March 23rd of the previous year. He is expected to return there soon. The writer states that it was believed the Japanese forces in charge of the camp had been planning a massacre of all the prisoners on the day the rescue occurred. The camp’s population was over 2,000, which included two bishops, 150 priests, and 125 nuns.

While imprisoned, the group had maintained daily religious observances, including the rosary and Benediction, as well as a Pontifical Mass every Sunday, in the hope of being rescued without a major violent event. Conditions in the camp were severe; most prisoners were so malnourished that they had difficulty walking, and approximately 20 people died from starvation.

The position of a porter, despite its associated dangers, offers many advantages. These benefits are accessible to individuals who maintain good will and cooperate with the divine grace that is understood to be unfailingly available from God and the Blessed Mother.

At times, this work can become monotonous and extremely boring, leading to a feeling of near collapse. In such situations, the passage advises that it is helpful to remember the example of Jesus. Specifically, it notes that even when he was about to fall for the third time, he patiently and without exception consoled the women and children of his persecutors.

The text asserts that one should be deeply grateful for such a vocation and for holding these privileged positions, including within the Franciscan Order (referred to as the Seraphic Order of the Poverello of Assisi). The passage concludes by expressing gratitude for God's divine patience with people.

In response to a communication from August 29, the following points are made regarding personal difficulties and religious faith.

The recipient's many difficulties are acknowledged. However, these experiences, which are typically considered misfortunes, are presented in a positive light. The underlying belief is that hardship is a sign of God's love, based on the principle that God disciplines those he loves. It is advised that if a person maintains a positive disposition and accepts the hardships that God sends or allows, these challenges will eventually be revealed as blessings.

The topic then shifts to a young acquaintance named Philip. The writer had previously hoped that Philip might have a special religious calling, or vocation. It is noted, however, that determining one's calling is a personal and often sensitive issue.

Regardless of a specific vocation, the hope is expressed that Philip will develop a sincere appreciation for his faith. This appreciation should begin with a theoretical understanding of the theological concept of the "Trace of the Trinity in the soul." Following this foundation in Faith, the other key virtues are Hope, which is described as the source of happiness in earthly life, and Charity (love), which is described as the essence and ultimate reward of eternal life.
styled: I just came across your favor of Aug. 29th on the con- viction that: "Whom the Lord loveth He Chastened", and even while I surely sympathize with you, in your so many difficulties, I do, nevertheless congratulate you on all these experiences that the crazy world considers such mis- forrtunes. If we only try to show the dear Lord a good will and ask Him for grateful resignation to the crosses He sends or permits to come our way, we may be sure that sooner or later they will turn out to have been just so many bless- ings,in disguise. I hoped for quite a time that my "little boy-friend Philip" might have a vocation to some thing special. That, however is a personal problem and in many cases seems to be a very delicate question. I hope of course, that he be earnestly appreciative of the holy Faith - theoretically first of the outstanding "Trace of the Trinity in our souls. The other two, hope and being essentially one with it - hope the soul of happiness in this world, charity, the life and crown of everlasting glory. . . . .
