The writer acknowledges receiving a card and accompanying personal letters from the recipient a few days prior and expresses gratitude. The writer also mentions an intention to include a further token of appreciation but indicates they may not be able to locate it.

The letter reports on a significant celebration held the previous day for the name day of an individual named Brother Gabriel. At this event, a superior known as the Father Provincial publicly honored Gabriel. He praised Gabriel's skill, stating he was "becoming quite proficient as a linotypest," and formally thanked him for his work on behalf of the entire Province.

This event reminded the writer of the recipient and a message the recipient had sent to Brother Gabriel, which Gabriel appeared to appreciate.

The writer sends good wishes to the recipient and their associates, including a person named Solanus. The writer notes that Solanus caused a great deal of trouble for them during their time at a place called St. Bonaventure's. This leads the writer to reflect on the good fortune of only being responsible for one's own conscience.

Finally, the celebration prompted the writer to reflect on the value of contributing to the general welfare through small, individual actions. The writer believes this is particularly meaningful within a religious community, where each person performs their role without concern for the status or type of work involved.
styled: God bless you and yours, - including that poor sinner Solanus, who more than anyone else gave me trouble as long as I was in St. Bonaventure's - Isent it a mercy that we really need examine only one "pair of conscience"! Well I received your card a few days ago and thank you for the same as well as for the personal letters therewith. Intimation of further appreciation below, if I can find it for you. We had quite a celebration yesterday of Br. Gabriel's nameday. Father Provincial gave him a nice little "sendoff", praising his work as, "becoming quite proficient as a linotypest" and thanking him for his work in the name of the entire Province, etc. I thought of you rightaway and of your message to him, which he seemed to quite appreciate. At the same time something came to my mind of our ineffable privilege in doing the little things we are able to do for the general welfare - most especially in a religious com- munity - each one in his place without thought or distinction as to what the work may be.

The writer has been at a new assignment, which they consider a privilege, for one week. They note two upcoming personal milestones: the next day marks the 41st anniversary of their first Mass, and the day after that is the 21st anniversary of their 1924 arrival at St. Bonaventure's from Our Lady of Angels parish in Harlem. The writer expresses a deep sense of gratitude for these experiences, viewing them as blessings.

Turning to practical matters, the writer hopes that the middle room they previously occupied was not left in a state of excessive disorder. They express concern that they have given the recipient a difficult job by asking them to pack and send certain items. These items are described as being of no use to anyone else but of some convenience to the writer.

For shipping, the writer is uncertain if they brought a trunk with them from Harlem more than two decades ago. They advise that if such a trunk exists, it has little value, and that any available box would be a suitable, and possibly better, container.

The writer specifies one item to be sent: a box labeled "Letters" that is located on top of the wardrobe. This box contains letters from a "Fr. Edward."

Now I hope you have not found that middle cell that succored me so long in too hopeless disorder. The reasoning provided is that any person who is truly grateful for their own vocation will naturally pray for others to receive similar callings. Therefore, praying for more vocations is a sign of properly appreciating one's own.

Thus they will at once be doing real missionary work and insuring their own holy vocation - and perseverance therein. The author asks them to also pray as much as they can, specifically to express gratitude to God for the countless blessings and graces they have collectively received over the past 48 years. The author feels unable to express this gratitude adequately on their own.

These divine graces and mercies are described as a constant, all-encompassing presence that people are immersed in, often without fully realizing it, much like the air that surrounds and permeates them.

The passage makes the following claims:

*   It is difficult for human beings, during their earthly lives, to fully appreciate or be sufficiently grateful for the blessings they receive from God and other benefactors.
*   This state of striving for gratitude is a fundamental part of the spiritual journey that begins at baptism, which makes a person a "candidate for the Kingdom of Heaven."
*   Receiving the sacraments of the Church is a way to advance on this spiritual path. Each sacrament is a step forward, metaphorically representing a plea for spiritual approval.

The author expresses awe at the wonderful and numerous opportunities available for spiritual growth and concludes with expressions of immense praise for God.

Please have them all as much as conveinent - have them all - supply my want of appreciation and gratitude to God for the uncountable mercies and graces we have received these 48 years - graces and mercies that have, not only surrounded us but in which, without our half realizing it, we are continually immersed in God' merciful graces / like the air that permiates us. But after all that is what we became candidates for - candidates for the Kingdom of Heaven - when we were baptized; and every time we receive the Holy Sacraments of Mother Church we take another step forward, virtually pleading with our angels for another white bean at every step. How wonderful and how legion are our privileged opportunités ! Glory be to God a billion.

The writer sends greetings to a group of novices who have relocated from their former residence at St. Bonaventure. The writer describes this move as a kind of exile.

These greetings are also extended to Father Aloisius, who for the past three or four years was the writer's next-door neighbor at a location called Saint Felix's. The writer feels the absence of Father Aloisius more than is typical because of their long-standing connection; the writer knew him first when he was a novice and then again recently, after a period of 25 years or more.

The writer observes that such separations are a normal part of life, both within their religious order and in secular society. However, the writer claims that these partings are much more disappointing for people in secular life.

Best wishes and a blessing are sent to Father Aloisius and all the novices at their new novitiate, St. Francis. The writer expresses hope for a potential visit to St. Francis for a day or two before the summer ends, if circumstances allow.

In the meantime, the writer advises that everyone should pray for one another's continued spiritual conversion. They are also encouraged to follow Jesus's plea to pray that God, referred to as "the Lord of the Harvest," will send more people to serve in the ministry.

The writer is responding to a recent communication that requested information about the benefits of the Seraphic Mass Association. This request has prompted the writer to take action on a project they had been considering for many months. The writer expresses a belief that this idea, which they term an "inspiration," was allowed to persist through divine patience until the recipient's letter spurred them to make a decision.

In the writer's view, the benefits of the association are so numerous and evident that a comprehensive list would be too long for the short letter they have time to write. Therefore, the writer intends to provide a brief summary of these advantages.

As a primary example, the writer states that the Church highlights the association's importance by granting a 300-day indulgence to its promoters. This indulgence is granted for every person enrolled in the association. Furthermore, it is granted for any effort made to promote the association's interests, including actions as minimal as speaking a few words in its favor.

The passage offers the following advice and perspective:

*   **On Anxiety and Miracles:** It is not good to be overly anxious or to expect God to perform a miracle on one's behalf. The reason for this is that God is the only one with the power to create miracles.

*   **On Seeking Divine Help:** While one should not expect miracles, it is possible to encourage divine intervention by seeking the intercession of the saints and the Blessed Mother Mary.

*   **An Example for Encouragement:** The case of Father Exprovincial Theodosius is offered as a source of hope. When he was a cleric, it was generally believed that his health was so poor he would not survive to be ordained.

*   **Advice for the Recipient:** A person named Father Sebastian is advised to maintain courage by focusing on living one day at a time. He should entrust the past and the future to God.

*   **A Final Request:** The writer asks Father Sebastian to pray for them, referring to themself as a sinner.

For more information, the reader is directed to page 13 of an included booklet.

To illustrate this point, a specific example from the association's records is provided:

In August, a woman identified as Mrs. B., who was anxious about her son's upcoming overseas deployment, enrolled him in the "Seraphic Mass." An office note dated October 5, 1945, clarifies that Mrs. Fred Brewer reported enrolling her son Fred, his comrade, their ship's crew, and others.

The ship they were on crossed the Atlantic Ocean successfully. However, two hours before its scheduled landing, it struck a mine, causing the ship and its cargo to sink. Despite this, all 2,500 men on board survived. The ship's captain reportedly described the complete survival of the crew as "miraculous."

The passage concludes by signaling a transition to a new topic concerning "possibilities and obligations."

### **Membership Eligibility and Purpose**

Membership in this association is open to anyone. It is intended for two main groups:
*   Individuals, including both atheists and believers, who are seeking spiritual conversion.
*   Those who are already devout and wish to achieve further spiritual growth and progress.

The organization defines religion as "the science of our relationship with God and our neighbor," and also notes that it involves a dependence on both.

### **Member Obligations**

The obligations for members are practical and are divided into spiritual and financial categories.

**1. Spiritual Duties:**
Active members are encouraged to perform two actions:
*   Pray for the organization's missions, its missionaries, and all other members of the association.
*   When possible, offer Holy Communion with these same intentions in mind.

**2. Financial Contributions:**
Members who are financially able are asked to contribute money to support the organization. The suggested amounts are:
*   **For living members:** 50 cents for an annual membership or a one-time payment of $5 for a perpetual membership. Larger contributions are welcome.
*   **For deceased members:** A contribution of $2 or more provides a perpetual membership for a deceased person.

### **Benefits of Membership**

Members receive both direct and indirect spiritual benefits.
*   **Direct Benefits:** Members are included in the intentions of approximately 525 Holy Masses celebrated every day, which totals about 188,500 Masses per year.
*   **Indirect Benefits:** In addition to the direct benefits, members also participate in all the good works of the entire religious order, which includes thousands of other Holy Masses celebrated daily.

The passage makes the following points:

A person's difficult situation is acknowledged as unique. However, the text immediately suggests that every individual's life is unique and distinct, just as no two grains of sand or stars are exactly alike.

This principle of uniqueness applies to the course of a person's life, which will inevitably contain a full range of experiences. These include very positive events, compared to rainbows and sunbursts, as well as extremely difficult hardships, described as "hellstorms." It is expected that a person will encounter this entire spectrum of events before life ends.

Death is portrayed as a peaceful conclusion, like a tired child going to sleep. This peaceful end is considered to be achieved through divine grace. The events of life, even when incomprehensible, are framed as part of a divine plan.

The central piece of advice is that it is never justifiable to feel bitter toward other people. According to the text, the only person one may justifiably direct bitterness toward is oneself.
styled: God bless you and yours. Praised be His Holy Name in all His unsearch- able designs! I read your pathethic oetter this morning and again just now. Yours is certainly a peculiar case. .... But after all, whose case is not a peculiar one? As no two grains of sand can be found exactly alike on all the strands of the oceans and as "star differeth from star in glory", so the ups and downs of this"life". So too the rainbows, the sun bursts, gentle breezes and the real Hellstorms we are liable to meet before, by the grace of God, we shall be able to tumble into our graves with the confidence of tired Children into their places of peaceful slumbers. But dear Sister; we are never justified in being "bitter" toward anyone except ourselves.

Nonetheless, one is only justified in feeling bitterness towards oneself, never towards others.

The passage makes the following points regarding a person identified as Sister Mary Joseph:

Those in positions of authority often have reason to regret their decisions, facing miscalculations and disappointment even with the most promising individuals, in addition to those whose suitability was always questionable.

In the case of Sister Mary Joseph, there were signs in her infancy and teenage years that suggested she had the potential to be appreciative and receptive to divine guidance. Based on this promise, she was given dedicated care and nurturing. The alternative, the text suggests, would have been to abandon her or to send her into the world inexperienced and vulnerable to exploitation by immoral people. She was instead cared for as if it were a required duty.

Despite this history of care, her current attitude is described as bitterness.

The author’s central advice to her is that she, like many others, needs to cultivate more appreciation for what has been done for her. She is told to be thankful to God for it. Furthermore, she is reminded of the Fourth Commandment, which mandates honoring one's parents. The passage asserts that in her situation, her superiors have fulfilled this parental role for a long time and are therefore owed the same respect.

According to the passage, a person can only achieve a certain state of spiritual well-being through individual effort. This effort depends on the quality of hope, which must be inspired by faith in God and strengthened by a confident belief in God's mercy and goodness.

The author contrasts this spiritual state with the simple act of "enjoying life in the world," which is presented as something entirely different and problematic.

To illustrate this point, the author uses the biblical story of Eve as a primary example. The passage notes that the Bible does not state how long Eve entertained temptation from Satan before eating the forbidden fruit. The author speculates that this period could have been as long as a hundred years, a timeframe presented as probable. The purpose of this speculation is to emphasize the vast amount of time Eve could have enjoyed paradise, far longer than the intended reader has been a nun, highlighting the magnitude of what she lost.

The author argues that the fall could have been avoided. If Eve had focused on reason, been grateful for her existence and her pure spiritual abilities, and appreciated the favor she had from heaven and earth, she would not have had the opportunity to indulge in what is described as "unprofitable curiosity" and discontent. The passage claims that the devil consistently promotes such discontent within flawed human nature.

The author concludes that Eve's story is a tragedy for all of humanity, identifying the root cause of her fall and the subsequent sorrows of humankind as ingratitude. This pattern of failure is then extended to contemporary religious figures. The author states that members of religious orders, such as the Sisters of Saint Francis, also frequently make mistakes, implying they are susceptible to the same fundamental errors.

But O! "to enjoy life in the world" is another thing. How long your Great .... Grandmother Eve dilidallied with Satan before she finally reached for the fatal apple, Holy Scripture does not tell. If it were a hundred years, which is easily probable, she would have enjoyed the original Paradise ten times as long as you've been a nun. Ead she listened to reason and been appreciative for her creation and the unsullied faculties that graced her soul and caused all on earth and in Heaven to smile in her direction, she would never have had time to give way to unprofitable curiosity or to dis- content that the devil never fails to foster in our tainted nature. But alas! ! ! Poor Eve's sad story! Poor Humanity's sorrows! Ingratitude! Poor Sisters of Saint Francis too! we might add; and poor religious of every other order! How often they make mistakes!

To offer hope, the writer states that they have previously received reports that were significantly worse than the news about Patrick, yet those situations had remarkably positive outcomes after months of anxiety and uncertainty. Based on these past experiences, the writer remains hopeful for good news.

The writer confirms that, as requested, they have enrolled Patrick in the Seraphic Masses and states that a favorable report would therefore not be a surprise. They intend to pray and hope, trusting in God for the best possible outcome.

A perspective from a faith-based viewpoint is offered for comfort. This perspective reframes what secular society might consider the worst outcome as a spiritual victory. This idea is supported by the principle, attributed to Jesus, that the greatest possible act of love is for a person to give their life for their friends. The writer suggests that this viewpoint ought to be a source of strength, especially during a time when many people are experiencing similar bereavements.

I just came to yours of the 23nd and sure do sympathize with you and your family. However, we've had so many decidedly worse reports than about your Pat, that turned out most remarkable after several months of suspence and anxiety, that I shall still hope for a good word about Son Patrick F. At all events I have just enrolled him in the Seraphic Masses as requested and we shall not be surprised at any favorable report to come. We'll pray and hope - trusting in God for the best. After all if we look at things in light of faith, the worst, as the world considers things, is only cur Victory - according to our dear Lord's own words: "Greater love than this no man hath that a man give his life for his friends". God bless you again, and love to all the family and friends.

Membership in this association is presented as the explanation for the effectiveness of certain powerful prayers that were discussed in Barclay Street, New York. An anecdotal account, taken from a collection of records called "Notes and Favors" compiled over several years, is offered as an example for Mr. Peters and his friends.

The account describes the case of Mrs. Catherine Nagle, a 45-year-old mother of eight. Two weeks prior, on May 9, she underwent surgery at Providence Hospital. Upon operating, the doctor discovered her cancer was so extensive that no procedure was attempted. The surgeon closed the incision, concluding that her condition was terminal and that she would not leave the hospital alive.

After Mrs. Nagle was enrolled in the Seraphic Mass Association, her husband asked if there was anything else he could do for her. He was advised to also enroll the "Poor Souls," while specifically keeping his own deceased relatives in mind. The husband agreed to this suggestion and made a special donation.

The story is shared with the intent of encouraging others to be persistent and dedicated in their prayers.

3.  This donation can be a formal enrollment for the "Poor Souls" or a contribution to another charitable cause.
4.  This promised action is intended to be in addition to other religious practices, such as prayers and receiving Holy Communion.

According to Christian teachings, supported by religious history and the natural world, there is no reason to be discouraged. Discouragement is presented as a sign of weakened faith.

Instead of discouragement, a negative experience should be viewed as a valuable opportunity to be thankful. It provides a chance to practice and develop humility. Furthermore, by expressing gratitude in advance for any future difficulties, a person can build confidence in divine wisdom.

Confidence in God is the essence of prayer, and it is typically achieved through trials and humiliations. A personal failure, even a seemingly minor one, is a significant hardship, or "cross," for an individual to bear.

To help develop this confidence, a specific verse is offered for consideration: "God condescends to use our powers, If we don't spoil His plans by ours." This suggests that God is willing to use human abilities, but that human plans can interfere with divine ones.

The author asserts that God's plans are always for the best and are wonderful. For individuals who are patient, humble, and trusting, these plans are described as being exceptionally holy and sublime.

The author suggests that the recipient may be overlooking a spiritual purpose or expectation related to their struggles. God sometimes mercifully sends or permits events to occur in people's lives to remind them of their ultimate purpose. As rational beings, this purpose is to know the Creator and to unite one's existence with the divine through eternal love and service.

A person's extensive charitable work is acknowledged as an indicator of their faith and charity, which may be greater than others perceive. However, properly prioritized charity begins with oneself. In this context, this means focusing on the internal cultivation of the supernatural virtues of faith, hope, and charity, which are considered to be essentially one virtue.

This internal focus requires a continuous effort to learn more about God in three aspects: as Creator, Redeemer, and Sanctifier. The reason for this emphasis on knowledge is that appreciation and love for anything or anyone are proportional to one's understanding of them. Just as one's love for a good person grows as one gets to know them better, knowledge of God is the necessary foundation for loving God.
styled: Hence the Good God, often in His mercy, sends something - at least permits it - to come to us for the purpose of waking us up, lest we forget the final purpose of our exist- ence as rational creatures, viz. to know our CREATOR and, in love and service to blend our existence with His for all eternity. Of course, I know that you have been doing a lot of charity-work these past years and I have thanked God to see it. It indicates to me at least, that you have more faith and more charity than many would like to concede. After all, however, rightly ordered charity begins at home. That means, in my figuering at least, the cultivation and fostering in our own individual hearts and souls the supernatural virtues of faith, hope and charity - essencially one virtue. In other words I might say it means for me personally, that I should strive continually to learn more and more about God my Creator, about God as my Redeemer, about God my Sanctifyer. Because in only as much as I know anything can I appreciate it. as I know a good person can I love him.

Both reason and a sense of gratitude for one's existence compel an individual to make the study of their relationship with the Creator their primary and most important focus. This pursuit should engage all of a person's mental abilities, in all circumstances, and throughout their entire life as a rational being. This gratitude is a response to the perceived, nearly infinite manifestations of the Creator's wisdom, power, goodness, and love.

The passage anticipates that some might question whether such a field of study, or "science," truly exists. It argues in response that if such a science is not possible, then rational creatures cannot exist either.

This claim is justified by the following reasoning: The first and most certain sign of intelligence is gratitude for benefits that have been received. Since the very first benefit a creature can receive is its own creation—as a creature cannot create itself—it follows that a rational being's existence is fundamentally linked to this capacity for gratitude. Therefore, the existence of intelligent beings implies the validity of studying the relationship with their source of existence.

The author acknowledges that the recipient, Dr. Koch, does a great deal for the community, much of which goes unknown, unacknowledged, or is met with disbelief by other people.

However, the author raises the possibility that God expects something more from the recipient. This additional expectation is a more serious focus on securing the salvation of their own soul.

The author's reasoning follows a principle of "rightly ordered charity." While charity towards others is always good and should be encouraged, true charity should begin "at home." The author interprets this to mean it should start within a person's own heart or soul.

The argument is based on the following theological premises:
1.  The primary purpose of a rational person's existence is to know their Creator.
2.  The reason for knowing the Creator is to be able to love and serve Him.
3.  The ultimate goal is to unite one's own existence with God's in eternal glory, which is achieved by cooperating with divine grace.

Based on this, the author concludes that a person's first obligation, and therefore their first act of charity, is to fulfill their duty of gratitude to God. This is best accomplished by making a conscious effort to recognize God, which in turn allows a person to intelligently appreciate and express that appreciation.

From these premises, the passage concludes that atheism is inexcusable according to the standards of reason and decency. The implication is that because atheism does not express gratitude to a creator for the benefit of existence, it fails a fundamental test of intelligence.

The author states that a "fearful" definition of atheism will follow, which is intended to further clarify and answer why atheism is without excuse.

The text claims that atheism is adopted by three types of individuals:

3.  Those who are profoundly foolish to the point of being "damned."

The first and immediate destructive consequence of adopting atheism is said to be the loss of supernatural hope, which the author defines as the essential source of happiness in life. This loss of happiness is explained by the inability to fulfill what the passage calls the "obligation of gratitude." Without a higher power to be grateful to, a person loses the primary practical foundation for happiness.

The author is writing to an acquaintance named Walter McClellan, who is currently experiencing some form of trouble. This situation reminds the author of their first meeting years prior, which also occurred when McClellan was in trouble. At that time, McClellan made a commitment referred to as "taking the pledge," which the author believed was the start of a good friendship, though they now express some doubt about this.

The author states that they have often thought of McClellan since that time and are grateful he has kept his pledge. However, the author has also frequently wondered what McClellan (referred to by the nickname "big W. Mack") is missing by not believing in religion, God, and Jesus Christ.

The author asserts with certainty that McClellan would be a different and altogether happier person if he had religious faith. This faith is described as the same one that has provided comfort and support to millions of people throughout history.

Finally, the author states that their own high respect for McClellan serves as proof that he cannot be a true atheist. The only exception imagined is the paradoxical case of an atheist who would thank God for their atheism.

The author of the passage feels a sense of duty, as both a friend and a grateful patient, to warn a person named Doctor Young about what the author perceives as a serious danger in his life.

The author's concern is based on the belief that a family is the greatest natural blessing that God provides. This point is illustrated with a recent anecdote about a middle-aged couple, who are also friends with Doctor Young. This couple expressed their sadness about being married for several years without having children.

The author then applies this theme to Doctor Young's own situation. The problem identified is not that Doctor Young lacks a family, but that the family he does have is without a "head." This implies that Doctor Young is failing to properly lead or fulfill his role within his family unit, which the author also considers to have been a blessing from God.

In conclusion, the author views this as a sad situation. Although such cases may be common, the author believes that from a divine or religious perspective, it is a very serious and regrettable problem.
styled: Hence, Dear Doctor Young: I feel that I would not be your friend or even a decently grateful patient were I to be silent as to dangers ahead of you as I see them without any doubt. Only yesterday a middle-aged couple - friends of yours too - lamented to me that after several years in holy matrimony, they had never been blessed with - what I have long since considered the greatest blessing that, in the natural order, God gives on earth, A Family. And my Doctor Young has no family. ? Because the family that God blessed him with has no head. ? At all events, it is a sad situation; and notwithstanding the fearful prevalence of similar cases, it must be, in the sight of Heaven a most lamentable problem.

He works in the cause of justice, truth, and religion, which is defined as the basis for a positive relationship with God and other people. His work is positioned in opposition to atheism, which is described as a form of intellectual and spiritual insanity. At times, his efforts have been internationally acknowledged.

However, he is also seen as being approximately fifty years ahead of his generation. The author believes that if Dr. Kraus perseveres and aligns his work with divine will and good intentions, his heroic struggle will yield great results.

A similar hope is expressed for the future of a person named Rickey Grix, who is described with affection and concern. This hope is held in spite of certain "scientific conclusions," just as the confidence in Dr. Kraus's success is maintained in the face of opposition from political atheism. This expresses a belief in a positive outcome for both individuals, even though God's plans are considered difficult to understand.

While the son seemed intelligent and aware, the author was disturbed by his behavior, which was perceived as showing a lack of respect for his father. This display was so pronounced that the author felt an urge to intervene and remind the son of the commandment to "Honor thy father and thy mother."

Upon reflection, the author attributes the son's behavior to the family's circumstances. The author describes the doctor as an "absentee father," notes that the mother is a "convert," and characterizes the family as "half-divorced." The author questions who is to blame for this situation.

The author's primary purpose is to convey that they have been continually thinking about how to resolve this family's problems. The specific goal is to find a way to introduce "Christian peace and harmony" into the family and ultimately bring the father and the entire family back together.

He seemed promisingly bright and alert; but what pained me as the little dialogue proceeded was the sad want of filial reverence and even respect shown to his father. *   Carefully and conscientiously nurtured by loving parents and teachers, who were acting as part of a divine plan.

The author claims that this guilt of neglecting one's faith is universal and that no person can claim to be exempt from it.

Following this, a logical argument is made for a specific course of action. Citing the idea that gratitude is a key indicator of intelligence, the passage argues that the only logical, intelligent, and holy response is for people to acknowledge their own shortcomings. These shortcomings are characterized as weakness, foolishness, and profound guilt in the eyes of God.

The conclusion is that the remedy for this guilt is a humble acknowledgement of these failings. This act of admission is presented as a mercifully simple and easy solution.

### Analysis of the Situation and Recommended Actions

**Current State and Proposed Solution**
The person being addressed is experiencing an unnatural fear and dislike of things they once loved and held sacred. The recommended course of action to remedy this is to return to a state of divine grace by making a good and humble confession.

**Predicted Outcome**
If this action is taken, the negative feelings of fear and dislike are expected to weaken immediately. Over time, it is highly probable that the individual will gradually return to their former, happier self.

**Warning Against the Current Path**
Continuing on the current path is described as extremely dangerous. This path is characterized as living in a probable state of mortal sin while procrastinating about the possibility of one day obtaining divine grace and eternal salvation.

**Urgent Analogy**
This current behavior is considered a dangerously close imitation of the actions of a previously mentioned "unfortunate judge." This parallel is a matter that requires urgent self-assessment and correction at all costs.

**Intent of the Message**
The purpose of this advice is not to be overly harsh or to cause discouragement. Instead, it is intended as an urgent warning to awaken the individual from a threatening state of spiritual complacency before it is too late.

**Shared Need for Support**
The writer also states their own need for prayers, identifying as a sinner who requires them just as anyone else does.

For a rational being, the effort to do what is right and the effort to be happy are fundamentally the same.

The primary requirement for any person is to make a genuine effort. The success of that effort is not determined by the individual but depends on God. However, God judges whether people have used the specific means and opportunities provided to them. It is expected that these means will be used to secure the success that divine justice requires.

It is claimed that very few people recognize this obligation. This failure is presented as the direct cause of a lack of inner peace for individuals. This personal unrest is then identified as the source of broader turmoil within families, nations, and the international community.

The passage concludes that while everyone naturally seeks peace with the same certainty as an object seeks rest, a rational person can only find this peace through the willing service of their Creator.

The author states that the doctor has used his abilities, which are described as God-given talents, in a praiseworthy manner. The author asks if the doctor has, in turn, been blessed by God and felt, at least temporarily, a sense of gratitude for the capacity to serve both a divine purpose and humanity.

A central question is then posed: Is the doctor content to continue living this way, motivated only by personal satisfaction and worldly benefits? These worldly advantages are characterized as superficial, including the approval of a public that does not think deeply.

The author presents these questions with the understanding that the doctor is an intelligent person capable of reasoning and, from a divine perspective, cannot claim ignorance of these matters.

The doctor is warned against continuing to implicitly reject what the author calls "the Church of the Living God" before it is too late. This rejection is described as a process of numbing one's conscience with the "poison of modern atheism." The author characterizes modern atheism as the ultimate form of intellectual and moral insanity, whose core belief is that a person can live a meaningful life without the Church and its sacraments, and therefore without God. The passage ends by challenging the very possibility of managing without the Church.

To be a peacemaker, a person must first humbly confess their own sins. The principle that "charity begins at home" applies here, with the "home" being the individual's soul. Peace is a primary characteristic of charity, and for these qualities to be genuine, they must first be established in the relationship between an individual and God.

This dependence on God is based on several principles:
*   Human beings can achieve nothing without divine assistance.
*   A person is either aligned with God or against God; there is no neutral position. Anyone not working with God is actively undermining God's purpose.
*   Listening to God's designated representatives is equivalent to listening to God.

A logical argument is presented to explain the absence of peace:
1.  The first punishment for sin is the withdrawal of divine grace.
2.  This withdrawal of grace is defined as the Holy Spirit departing from the sinner's soul.
3.  Peace is considered a primary gift of the Holy Spirit.
4.  Therefore, when a person sins, they lose the gift of peace.

This principle is then applied to a family situation. If a parent defies a divinely appointed representative of peace, that act is a sin. Consequently, it should not surprise any informed observer that there is a scandalous lack of peace in that parent's home. It is also an expected outcome that every immediate member of that family will be upset by this situation.

In such a home, one cannot expect to find positive faith being fostered or appreciated, nor an understanding of the moral obligations that apply to rational human beings. The passage concludes by asserting that it is a self-evident philosophical truth that reason, moral obligation, appreciation, and religion are all necessarily and inseparably linked.

The passage establishes a foundational principle using two biblical verses: any human endeavor, such as building a house or protecting a city, is ultimately futile and done in vain unless it has divine support from God.

Based on this principle, the writer addresses a specific person with the following points:

1.  **Motive:** The writer's intention is not to cause embarrassment. On the contrary, the writer feels a duty as a friend to intervene in order to prevent a definite and severe embarrassment that the recipient is otherwise certain to face.

2.  **The Problem and Solution:** The recipient is currently trying to operate without God. This path will lead to the predicted embarrassment. The only way to avoid this outcome is for the recipient to recognize this error and cease trying to live and work without God's help. This change is presented as something that happens "by the grace of God."

3.  **Justification:** The writer contrasts two scenarios to justify this immediate, friendly correction. The potential embarrassment of being corrected now is insignificant compared to the far greater humiliation of being publicly accused during a final, universal judgment before all of heaven, earth, and hell.

4.  **General Philosophy:** The writer concludes with a practical observation: when a real problem lies ahead, confronting it early minimizes its negative impact. Conversely, ignoring or downplaying a real problem will only make its consequences worse.

The author acknowledges that this religious message may be unpleasant to receive, comparing the experience to the discomfort of a dental procedure for both the dentist and the patient. The point is made that despite the unpleasantness, the process is necessary for a positive result.

The text then directly advises its reader, a doctor, to read the message patiently and to pray for understanding and goodwill. It claims that doing so will create a hopeful outcome for both the author and the reader. The promised benefits are said to be greater than fixing a physical problem like a tooth; they include achieving a worthwhile life on Earth and the salvation of one's immortal soul.

The passage concludes by invoking Saint Francis, who is described as humble and therefore powerful in his intercession (praying on behalf of others). Through this intercession, the author expresses a desire for the Lord to grant peace to the doctor and their family.

According to the passage, many people have a mistaken understanding of both religion and conversion.

The author defines conversion as the process of receiving divine grace and, as a result, returning to a more earnest and practical commitment to know, love, and serve God. This is presented as a continuous process applicable to everyone, based on the premise that all human beings are inherently sinful and imperfect. Therefore, any individual can always be "converted" from their less perfect ways.

The passage then outlines specific types of conversion for different groups:
1.  People outside of Christianity, such as followers of paganism or Judaism, can be converted to Christianity.
2.  Christians who are not Catholic, referred to as "good protestants," already believe in Jesus Christ. For them, conversion is a process of leaving their "errors" and what the author calls "human, therefore erroneous, systems of religion."
3.  This conversion leads them to what is claimed to be the "one and only divinely established" system: the Catholic Church, which is identified as the "true Church of Jesus Christ."

To support this view, the author distinguishes between "religion" and "systems of religion." Religion is likened to a science, meaning a single, unified body of truth. Based on this premise, there can only be one true religion. In contrast, there can be many different "systems of religion," which are human attempts to structure or practice that truth. This distinction is used to argue that while numerous religious systems exist, only one—Catholicism—is the true, divinely founded religion.

It seems to me, therefore, that to be converted means to receive the grace of God, one way or other, to come back more and more earnestly and more practically to know, to love and to serve God. And since we are all so inclined to go rong and to sin - even born in sin -- we can always be converted (in the wider sense), from our less perfect ways: and if outside the true Church, people can be converted from paganism and Judaism to Christianity. If they already believe in Jesus Christ as so many good protestants do, they can be converted from their errors and from human, therefore erroneous systems of religion, to the one and only divinely established founded system, viz, the Catholic systom or true Church of Jesus Christ. Let me stress here the expression, systems of religion, because if as above defined, religion is a science, there can be but one religion, whereas there may be a thousand different systems.

Upon hearing this account, the Father Provincial called it "quite a remarkable case."

Based on this belief in Saint Anthony's personal investment in Jack, the author advises that they should all pray for the saint's intercession with confidence and persistence. The stated goal is to ensure that Saint Anthony finishes the work he is believed to have started when he first inspired Jack.

The author of the passage just received a letter dated February 9th, which had been forwarded from St. Bonaventure's in Detroit. The author expresses a belief that the circumstances of receiving the news are evidence of a wonderful divine plan.

The letter contained a report about "Jack's Few Years" and informed the author that the letter's recipient and a Mrs. Turrell both received their First Holy Communion on Christmas. This news delighted the author, exceeding their hopes and moving them to tears, both upon reading the letter and while writing about it.

The author reiterates the congratulations they had previously offered to the recipient in a long-distance phone call on the night of the event. They clarify that these congratulations are also meant for Mrs. Turrell with the same sincerity. The author regrets not speaking to Mrs. Turrell directly during that phone call but reasoned at the time that it was more appropriate to thank God, who the author believes is the source of such happiness and blessings.

The author notes they were at St. Bonaventure's on the night of the First Communion, which enabled them to receive the news directly by phone. The next day, they shared the information with others at dinner, and those individuals were also very pleased.

On a Tuesday afternoon, a Catholic neighbor introduced the distressed Mrs. W. to the narrator. Mrs. W. stated her willingness to do anything to please God if her husband were spared.

In response, she was advised to make a proposition to God in a manner consistent with her own Methodist faith. The specific terms of this proposition were that if her husband showed a surprising recovery by the next day or by the end of that week, she would earnestly investigate the relationship between her denomination and the Catholic Church, which was referred to as the "Mother Church."

The following day, Wednesday, Mr. W. was discharged from the University Hospital in Ann Arbor. His doctors, identified as Wood and Pete, pronounced his recovery to be miraculous.

That Friday, both Mr. and Mrs. W. returned. Mr. W., though bandaged, was smiling.

It then makes the point that Judas was an Apostle and Lucifer was an archangel, and both fell from grace. This serves as a warning that even a high former status provides no security for one's present or future spiritual condition.

The narrator and several siblings, including one who became a clergyman, were baptized at a specific location.

The narrator mentions a man, the husband of a woman whose maiden name was Kathleen C'Brien. This man was described as an "atheist" because he had received little to no religious education in his childhood and, as a result, had never joined a religious denomination. However, he was a person of good moral character.

Influenced by his wife's exemplary behavior and the peaceful, prayerful atmosphere she cultivated in their home, the man came to admire her religious faith. He saw it as a source of hope and charity.

This couple had a son who drowned in Chicago on his seventh birthday. At the time, the family was traveling to an event called the Jubilee. They transported the boy's body with them and buried him in his mother's family plot.

This grave is situated near the burial site of the narrator's two younger sisters. Both sisters died within the same week in 1878, when the narrator was eight years old.

The writer acknowledges receiving an interesting letter from the recipient. From this letter, the writer concludes that the recipient must be managing reasonably well, despite grieving the recent death of his wife, Mercile, whom he described as patient.

The writer expresses regret for not having been able to see Mercile before she died. The writer clarifies that the purpose of such a visit would have been to encourage her in qualities such as faith, hope, charity, patience, resignation, and confidence in God. The writer reflects that it is a privilege and a source of happiness to assist someone in their final moments, especially by offering an encouraging prayer when things seem hopeless.

Based on the recipient's description of Mercile's life, including her struggles and humiliations, the writer believes she had learned the important art of "dying well."

As a related point, the writer mentions an anecdote from ten years prior. An in-law, whom the writer describes as an "atheist," lost his eldest child while the family was on their way to the 75th anniversary celebration of his wife's parish, St. Joseph's, in Prescott, Wisconsin.
styled: God bless you and yours. I hope you are well, as evidently you are not too bad to write such an interesting letter as that which I have just read from your pen. And all notwithstanding your trying berievement of losing your dear, patient Wife Mercile. I surely would like to have seen her and consoled her before it were too late. Rather I should say, to encourage her in her acts and disposi- tions of faith, hope, charity, patience, resignation, confidence in God etc. What a privilege; what a happiness to have been of assistence to anyone in their final struggle and to have whispered an encouraging prayer into the ear of the patient when naturally everything must seem dark and hopeless! From what you have written of her, however, with all her struggles and humiliations, etc, I think she must have learned quite a little of the one most important art of "dying well". Incidently, I had an "atheist" in-law lose his eldest born, ten years ago on his way with his family to the diamond jubilee of his wife's parish - St. Joseph's in Prescott, Wis.

This passage is a response to someone's expressed concerns, advising them not to be overly anxious about their situation.

The author makes an argument based on the concept of a divine plan for order. It begins with an analogy: just as well-organized people follow the principle of "a place for everything and everything in its place," there is a universal divine order. This human instinct for order is presented as a reflection of a divine characteristic, suggesting that God has a specific place and purpose for every individual.

The text asserts that although an all-powerful creator could accomplish things directly and bypass normal systems—for instance, by creating humans without parents, educating children without schools, or administering holy sacraments without priests—this is not the chosen method.

Instead, God's chosen system is to honor people by assigning them roles and tasks that suit their individual abilities. This involvement is described as a form of participation and cooperation in divine work.

The final conclusion is that since God has an orderly plan and is infinitely more concerned with and in control of any situation than any human can be, excessive worry is unnecessary.
styled: God bless you and yours. I have just read your favor of the 8th - pathetic enough in its way, though indicating nothing to be over anxious about. Good housekeepers and good busines-men are careful to have "a place for everything and everything in its place." In this they show a trace of the divine character of the universal Guide and Master, Who of course, has a place for each one of us. He, the Creator and Divine Governer of the universe in all its details, could create children as in the case of Adam and Eve without parents. He could teach little children without nuns or schools and give the holy sacraments as has been the case on several occasions, - without priests, therefore. In His divine economy, however, God has been pleased to honor His creatures- most especially His rationals - by giving them, each accord- ing to his ability, a part of His own work to do. Rather I ought to say, by participation and cooperation in His won divine activity, etc. Why be over anxious, therefore, about something that God himself is infinitely more solicitous than any of His creatures can be?

The writer of a letter received weeks prior had repeatedly attempted to enroll someone, described by the letter's recipient as a "hopeless case," into the Seraphic Mass Association. These attempts failed because the individual's name was not provided, causing the writer to postpone the enrollment.

To offer advice on the matter, the writer shares a story about a different case. The intent is that the recipient will understand the recommended course of action from this example.

The story is as follows: On the morning of Saturday, January 10, 1925, the recipient's parents were brought by a neighbor from Port Huron to the St. Bonaventure Monastery in Detroit. The father, a Mr. Eagen, was so ill he could barely speak. He explained that doctors had diagnosed him with "stomach ulcers." The writer later discovered that the doctors had actually diagnosed him with terminal cancer and had sent him home, viewing his case as hopeless.

The writer then explained the Seraphic Mass Association to Mr. Eagen and suggested that he do something for the missions. Having learned his name, the writer offered him the option of perpetual enrollment in the association.

The writer expresses gratitude for a generous communication sent on October 16th and specifically for being enrolled in an association. This is one of approximately a dozen perpetual enrollments the writer has received during the current Jubilee year, in addition to a large, uncounted number of annual enrollments. The writer's appreciation for these enrollments is based on the belief that continued positive outcomes, attributed to God, are reported through this association.

Regarding the adoption of children, the writer’s perspective is guided by the Christian principle, "What you have done for the least of my brethren You have done to me." This means that caring for the most vulnerable people is considered an act of service to Jesus.

The writer's clerical organization has 24 promising novices this year, a fact for which the writer expresses gratitude to God. There is a significant need for more priests for both domestic and international missions, and the organization could place at least a hundred more if they were available.

Finally, the writer congratulates the recipient for having joined the Franciscan order, which is described as a privileged group.

A man who seemed to be short of funds was advised to enroll in a program for only one year at first, with the understanding that he would commit to a permanent enrollment later if his situation improved. The man agreed to this.

At this initial meeting, the narrator estimated the man's age to be 75 or older and observed that his wife also looked old.

Eight days later, on a Sunday morning, the man drove his own car to follow through on his promise. His appearance, and that of his wife, had changed so dramatically that the narrator would not have recognized them by sight alone. The narrator only identified the man as the individual from Port Huron upon hearing him speak. The man looked 30 years younger than he had at their first encounter. His actual age at that time had been only 39.

The man then mentioned that doctors in Port Huron wanted to take an X-ray and asked the narrator for an opinion. The narrator inquired about the cost of the procedure, which was $25. The narrator then asked the man's wife for her thoughts. Both the man and his wife were smiling broadly. The wife exclaimed that her husband did not need the X-ray, pointing to his visibly improved condition as proof. The passage ends as the narrator begins to respond.

The recipient of the message is instructed to submit the name of a friend who is considered a "hopeless case." They are also instructed to arrange for as many people as possible to offer prayers and Holy Communions.

These religious observances are intended for two groups of people:
1.  The friend previously mentioned.
2.  Influential individuals ("big shots") in hospitals or other settings who are described as unfortunate. These individuals are characterized as having little or no faith in the supernatural and refusing to believe in the possibility of miracles.

The stated goal of these prayers is that an undeniable miracle might occur. Such an event could persuade these individuals who lack faith to begin praying for the gift of faith themselves. The passage concludes with the claim that God is waiting to grant the gift of faith as soon as it is requested.

A man made a promise regarding the souls in Purgatory, stating that if he managed to forget a particular appointment, he would dedicate a portion of some benefit to them. He enthusiastically committed to a fifty-fifty split. Following this, he drove to a specific location weekly for several months.

On February 29, while accompanied by others for whom he also customarily made offerings, he fulfilled his promise. He instructed a priest to formally credit the souls in Purgatory with more than half of a $25 sum, specifying a donation of $14.

Years later, the author of the passage visited an elderly woman in Smith's Creek who was dying of stomach cancer. The father of the letter's recipient heard of this visit and took the author to see a small farm. While there, the author saw a child named Dorothy and claims to have had a premonition at that time about her future religious vocation.

The recipient of the letter, identified as Sister M.C., is advised to appreciate her situation, which is described as an exceptional privilege. This privilege is defined as being chosen from among millions of people to be a spiritual spouse to the "eternal King of kings."

I'll go them fifty-fifty." After that he drove down every week for several months. Febr. 29th - I believe he had the whole Family down - having enrolled some other, as he nearly always did, he concluded about as follows: "Now Father; I want to enroll the Poor Souls as I promised them I would. Put them down for a good half of that $25. - fourteen dollars." This work is described as both a privilege and an arduous undertaking. The writer states a belief that the recipient has been and will continue to be divinely rewarded for their practical involvement in what is characterized as an important form of Catholic action.

Additionally, the writer commends the recipient for speaking so positively about a young male business associate. This occurred in the context of the recipient offering the young man condolences on the death of his mother. The writer finds it reassuring to hear about people of such good character. The fact that the young man was a "bible student" is seen as a positive indicator. However, the writer adds the caution that, without what is considered proper guidance, the study of the Bible can lead individuals to problematic or harmful conclusions.

I hope my tardiness may not scandalize. Not only this favor, however, do I want to thank you, but more I want to assure you of our appreciation of your generous activity these several years in the really privileged, though not less arduous work of the holy foreign missions. I am sure that the Good God will bless - has blessed - you in many ways for your practical interest in this outstanding phase of really Catholic action. Besides this, I want to congratulate you on your having been so guided as to be able to write of a business associate as you do of the young man with whom you condole on the death of his amiable mother. It is always a relief to know of such a person. The very fact of his having been a "bible student" ought to spell something in his favor. This, even though, for want of proper guidance, many a "bible student" has anchored in dangerous waters.

The passage presents a theological argument about suffering and scandal, applying it to the specific situation of an individual named Sister Agnes Carmel.

The central theological point, attributed to a figure named Bernard, is that after the crucifixion of Jesus Christ, no event should be considered a "scandal" in a way that shakes one's faith. The crucifixion is described as the most terrible scandal of all, yet God transformed it into the means of salvation for believers. This is used as evidence that God's plans and judgments are mysterious and beyond human understanding.

Applying this principle to Sister Agnes Carmel, the author asserts that based on her letter, her mind is sound. The author's interpretation is that her suffering is not a sign of a personal problem but is a mission being endured for several reasons:
1.  On behalf of other people, specifically her parents and family.
2.  For the purpose of her own humiliation.
3.  As a means to achieve her spiritual purification.

The author advises her to be thankful to God for this mission. It is further clarified that this mission was likely imposed on her by God, rather than simply offered, because she would not have had the courage to voluntarily accept the sacrifice it demanded.

The passage concludes by stating that this spiritual struggle is ongoing and that a victory over "the devil and scandal" has not yet been won.

Personal weaknesses and flaws serve a divinely intended purpose: they function as a natural safeguard against the arrogance and egotism to which talented individuals are particularly susceptible. For this reason, instead of being a source of regret, these weaknesses should be a cause for continuous gratitude.

This self-awareness includes understanding that these flaws are a consequence of sin. This divine grace is what distinguishes a person from secular or worldly individuals who lack faith. The passage claims that such people, without this insight into their own flawed nature, never learn how to engage in genuine, profound thought.

The passage proposes a specific relationship between knowledge, morality, and divinity. It argues that to truly know something is to appreciate it, which in turn leads to loving what is good, rejecting what is evil, and ultimately, adoring the divine. This understanding is presented as a source of significant comfort and hope.

The central claim is that the primary purpose of human creation is to know God. Keeping this purpose in mind is said to provide a positive and hopeful outlook, even for individuals who see themselves as imperfect or as "sinners." This idea is summarized with a set of related points: God created humans with the aim of being known by them; loving and serving God are natural consequences of this knowledge. For those who are grateful, pursuing this purpose is described as an earthly experience of heaven, and valuing it correctly is considered to be of the highest possible worth.

The text then anticipates a logical challenge: How can a finite human, limited by physical senses, come to know an incomprehensible God whose attributes—such as wisdom, power, goodness, and mercy—are infinite?

The passage concludes by suggesting that this complex question can, in the first instance, be addressed with a simple answer.
styled: To know is to appreciate - is to love what is good - is to reject what is of evil - is to adore the Divine. What consolation this offers us! What a hopeful outlook it ought to afford! What a sublime horizon for poor sinners, -- if "hope is the very soul of happiness here" and if the revealed purpose of our creation, TO KNOW GOD is kept in mind -- what a horizon for us, even though we be sinners -- if we but keep in mind the primary purpose of our creation, TO KNOW GOD. Hence the lines: God made me to know Him. O what a bless'd aim! To love Him and serve Him sure rests in the same. Its "Heaven Begun" for the grateful on earth; -- To treasure aright? ! Highest Heaven its worth. But how can I know what the senses fail to perceive? How know the Incomprehensible God whose attributes - wisdom and power and goodnes and mercy-are infinite? A simple question may, in the first place, demand a simple answer.

From these premises, the argument concludes that God's existence must be evident to any reasonable person. Consequently, every individual with the capacity for thought has both the ability and the obligation to recognize and worship the Creator.

This obligation is presented as having ultimate consequences. Failure to fulfill this duty will result in the loss of everything good and the damnation of one's soul, a state described in religious texts as being "cast out into exterior darkness, where there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth."

However, the passage then asserts that given the profound importance of this subject, it would be a grave error to be satisfied with only this minimum level of logical deduction. The author concludes that the preceding argument is ultimately insufficient and does not represent the full understanding that people ought to have, and which it is hoped they will one day achieve.

The passage begins with the proverb that a foolish person can ask a question or raise an objection that a wise person would find difficult to answer. The author extends this to include dishonest people, or "knaves," arguing that while not every fool is a knave, every knave is ultimately a fool.

This idea is then used to address a specific objection: the challenge or impossibility of a finite creature being able to know an infinite God.

The author proposes answering this objection with analogies:
1.  Do people perceive the electricity in a live wire with their senses?
2.  Do people stare directly into the sun to understand its benefits?

The point of these analogies is that it is possible for humans to know of and benefit from powerful things (like electricity or the sun) without being able to perceive or comprehend them directly or completely. By extension, it is therefore possible for a finite being to know God without fully comprehending His infinite nature.

The passage concludes with a strong judgment on such objections. It states that they are futile and pointless. If these objections are used as an excuse for atheism, the author considers them "criminal." The final claim is that there is absolutely no valid excuse for any rational being to refuse to recognize its Creator.

Hopefulness is an often-overlooked quality essential for both physical and spiritual well-being. Neglecting it is harmful to progress in both areas.

The primary historical example of this is the offense, or "scandal," that some of Jesus's disciples experienced regarding his choice of crucifixion as the means to establish his "Reign of love." They were scandalized that he chose this path of suffering rather than a more triumphant one. This is illustrated by the disciple Peter's objection, "Far be it from you, Lord!," which prompted Jesus's severe response: "Get behind me, Satan... You do not have in mind the concerns of God."

The passage asserts that this type of spiritual challenge was not meant to be confined to the apostolic era. It cites the prominent medieval theologian Saint Bernard, who taught that since the "scandal of the Cross," it is never reasonable to be scandalized by events. In other words, the crucifixion serves as the ultimate example of a divine plan working through apparent tragedy, so one should not lose faith when encountering other difficult circumstances.

A second example of the disciples taking offense is their reaction to Jesus's teaching that he is the "bread of life," which must be consumed for spiritual life. He contrasted this with the manna their ancestors ate in the desert, who ultimately still died. This teaching was also a source of scandal and disbelief for his followers.

The author departed from the Wayne area in a vehicle driven by an individual named Ignatius, accompanied by Brother Cook and Reverend Father Guardian.

Upon leaving Fort Wayne, their train was running 25 minutes behind schedule. This delay led the author to believe it would be very difficult to make the scheduled connection to the Hiawatha train in Chicago, especially if any more time was lost. However, after departing from Huntington, the author and their companions prayed the Rosary for guidance, protection, and a safe return. Following this, the author no longer felt worried about the delay.

They successfully made the connection in Chicago, as the departing train waited for a short period while a ticket was purchased for the author. The author had been operating under the assumption that the funeral was on Saturday and had planned to stay overnight in St. Paul. This plan changed upon arrival; as the first passenger off the train, the author was met by friends who informed them of a new itinerary.

The author had to re-board the train and travel with these friends to Minneapolis. From there, after a 90-minute wait, the plan was to take another train 200 miles further to Ortonville, Minnesota, a town near the South Dakota border. The following morning, the final arrangements were to attend Mass and then drive 20 miles to Graceville for the funeral at 10:00 AM.

This report covers a trip taken to attend the funeral of Father Maurice Joachim. The funeral was considered a solemn, yet positive and blessed occasion, and this account was started the day after the event.

News of the death came via a telegram from Ortonville, Minnesota, at about 7:30 AM on Wednesday, January 12. The message stated that Father Maurice Joachim had died at 6:20 AM that same morning. The writer initially, and incorrectly, assumed the funeral would be on Saturday. After waiting for further details until nearly midnight, a phone call came, but it was from a convert regarding an unrelated divorce matter.

The writer had made a long-distance call to a superior, who granted permission to travel to the funeral, for which the writer was grateful. It was then concluded that the funeral might take place on Friday, so a decision was made to travel without delay to avoid missing it.

The plan was to take the Hiawatha train, as it was considered the most reliable option for making the required connections. On Thursday morning, it was snowing, so the group left early from a location referred to as "Ft." to be certain of catching the Pennsylvania Railroad's "Golden Arrow" train.
styled: No doubt you will have been expecting a report of some kind con- cerning the privileged trip conceded me recently to the Funeral of poor, dear brother, Father Maurice Joachim. I started to do this the day after the solemnities; for all considered it was a real solemn funeral and seemingly a happy one. Blessed be God in His angels and in His saints. A wire at about 7:30 Wednesday, January 12 from Ortonville, Minn. announced to us: "Father Maurice Joachim died at 6:20 this Morning". I erroneously took it for almost self understood that the Funeral would take place on Saturday, waiting for more particulars till near midnight, when a call came; but it was from a poor party - convert - lamenting their unfortunate divorce. Your Very Rev. Paternity, on my long distance call had benignly bidden me go thither. Deo gratias. We concluded that possibly the funeral might be Friday and decided accordingly to take no chances. Hence, our plans to catch the Hiawatha as probably - surest train to make the desired connections. It snowed that Thursday morning and to be sure of catching the "Golden Arrow" train on the Pennsylvania, we left early, for Ft.

The author has been contemplating a "million-dollar proposition" for many months, starting even before a formal visit by a religious superior the previous year. The author feels that this project is increasingly timely, opportune, and urgent.

The project is a million-dollar essay contest, which has received an encouraging proposal from a benefactor named Joseph J. O'Donnell of Chicago. A copy of his letter is to be included with the author's correspondence. In addition to this specific support, a number of other people, believed to be mostly religious individuals, are praying for the contest's success.

The author has previously discussed this proposal with Mother Mary Fidelis of Notre Dame Milwaukee, who was a "helpless invalid" at the time, and with approximately fifty of her nuns. This discussion took place on the day a statue of Father Stephen was unveiled. Both Mother Mary Fidelis and the nuns seemed interested and promised to pray for the project to succeed.

On that same day, the author experienced a severe case of ptomaine (food) poisoning. Although the experience was physically unpleasant, the author considers it to have been spiritually beneficial. The author also expresses hope that students from a place called Calvary, who had a similar but less severe experience, also derived some benefit from it.

At the crucifixion, Jesus addressed his mother, Mary, and gesturing toward the Apostle John, said, "This is your son." According to the passage, theologians and early Church leaders have consistently taught that in this statement, John symbolically represented all followers of Jesus's teachings. Jesus then immediately said to John, "This is your mother."

The text presents two related arguments for exclusivity. First, it defines religion as "the science of our happy dependence on God and our neighbor" and claims this definition is universally accepted. Based on this premise, it concludes that there can be only one true religion. Similarly, it argues that since being a Christian is defined as believing in Jesus Christ and adhering to his doctrine, there can be only one true form of Christianity.

Therefore, the passage advises that each person has a responsibility to examine their conscience and determine if they are a Christian in reality or just in name. Furthermore, it suggests that individuals should view it as a positive opportunity to continually perfect themselves in this faith and to identify its infallible guide on Earth.

The author is responding to a distressing letter and expresses sympathy for the recipients regarding their child's diagnosis of blindness and deafness, acknowledging that this is a great disappointment for any parent.

The author hopes that the child, D.J., will defy the medical prognosis, suggesting that such positive outcomes are common for those who have faith in God.

The recipients are encouraged to recognize the positive aspects of their situation, which are presented as evidence of God's mercy. These points are that they have another healthy son and that the affected child, Donald, possesses other positive qualities and abilities.

The author then argues that physical or worldly blessings are less important than the spiritual gift of faith. This faith is described as a powerful, shared bond between the author and the recipients, which exists even if their specific religious beliefs differ on some points.

Expanding on this, the author claims that all who genuinely believe in and hope in God have a great deal in common. Because of this shared foundation, believers should be patient with the common weaknesses and imperfections found in the ways people or religious systems apply and practice their faith.
styled: My Dear Friends: God bless you and yours. God bless all our afflicted brethren of good (will). I received your pathetic letter yesterday and I surely do sympathize with you. What a disapointment to any loving parent to hear such a diagnosis. "Blindness, Deafness". I surely hope D. J. will give the doctors a surprise as nearly always happens when we trust in Almighty God. At all events how merciful has not God shown Him- self to you in blessing you with another bright boy, and even in Donald's case, otherwise endowing him with such happy faculties! And yet dear friends; what are all purely physical or temporal blessings in comaprason with the faith that God has given us? - You and me, even though (we) differ, as may be, in some essentials. Besides, we have somuch in common - and this we can say of all who honestly believe in God and hope in Him, that we ought surely to be patient with weaknesses so common, if not in systems of religion at least, in application and practice.

The author argues that this perceived threat should motivate believers to find mutual agreement and harmony. They should come together to encourage humanity to consider the consequences of a future without faith in God.

The intended purpose of his sight being restored is so that he can glorify God and be instrumental in promoting peace among people and nations.

The author puts forward a specific view of religion, claiming it is not only a science but the "greatest science of all ages." Based on this premise, it is argued that there can be only one true religion, which is defined as "the science of our happy relationship with—and dependence on—God and our neighbor."

The passage concludes by linking the problem of atheism to a failure to cultivate this "science" of religion. The author claims that most people, in their "blindness," refuse to even recognize religion as a science.

An individual named Constance has been readmitted to her religious order for the second time within a few months. This event is portrayed as a significant act of divine mercy. The condition for her return was simply to resume wearing the order's religious habit, an opportunity described as a greatly desired gift.

This situation is presented as being historically unique and a powerful demonstration of the Mother General's confidence in Constance, who is characterized as an unsteady or "wavering" member. This act of acceptance is considered more meaningful than any other works or deeds.

The writer suggests that a divine power was influencing the Mother General's decision and is actively arranging circumstances to make Constance's return easier, despite her past "infidelities" and general inconsistency.

The passage then warns that a malevolent spiritual force, an "enemy of souls," will try to create doubt and disrupt one's inner peace. It does this by prompting skeptical questions (framed as "If..." and "Why...") that suggest God's handling of individual circumstances might be flawed or motivated by something other than pure mercy, wisdom, power, and love. These doubting questions are compared to the deceptive reasoning used by the serpent in the biblical story of the Garden of Eden.

Finally, the passage concludes with a psychological observation: it is a natural human tendency to feel frustrated or disappointed when denied the chance to justify one's own actions. Accepting mercy requires admitting fault, which conflicts with this innate desire for self-justification.

Through careful intervention, observed by Guardian Angels, the Church, and the Heavenly Court, further self-humiliation is prevented. In a specific situation, an individual (referred to as "Sister") might have questioned why the Reverend Mother perceived her only in her holy habit. However, it is suggested that the appropriate response should have been wonder at the Mother's overwhelming gentleness and foresight, implying that this was Jesus once more removing difficulties and embarrassments.
